item.content:encoded:
Artificial intelligence is rapidly transforming how people work, communicate, access services, make decisions, conduct businesses, manage resources, and interact with institutions. Yet as AI systems become increasingly influential, questions about responsibility, human dignity, cultural identity, trust, safety, and governance have become equally important.

A new international initiative, Anima Mundi: The Soul of the World Meets the Machine, is inviting start-ups, industries, researchers, designers, engineers, founders, young people, and communities from around the world to explore how cultural traditions, mythologies, cosmologies, and lived experiences can contribute to the governance of artificial intelligence.

The initiative calls on participants to bring the wisdom embedded in their own cultures into contemporary conversations about AI. Through digital art and written descriptions, participants are encouraged to connect cultural stories and traditions with real decisions being made by AI companies and private-sector teams today.

The initiative is presented by the AI Hub for Sustainable Development, a G7-endorsed, MIMIT-UNDP co-led initiative focused on accelerating sustainable AI-driven growth in Africa in alignment with the Italy-Africa Mattei Plan.

What Is the Anima Mundi AI Call About?

The central idea behind the initiative is that responsible AI should not be shaped exclusively by engineers, companies, governments, or technical specialists.

Instead, the organisers argue that communities possess forms of cultural, moral, philosophical, spiritual, social, and historical knowledge that can contribute to how societies think about the power and responsibilities associated with AI.

The call therefore asks participants to explore the relationship between culture and artificial intelligence.

It specifically encourages submissions that bring forward:

  • Mythologies
  • Cosmologies
  • Living cultural traditions
  • Stories about power and responsibility
  • Experiences of dignity and domination
  • Traditions concerning care and reciprocity
  • Community experiences with technology
  • Cultural perspectives on responsible decision-making
  • Experiences of how AI affects people and communities

The objective is not to identify one universal cultural answer to AI governance. Instead, the initiative seeks to create a broader international dialogue in which different communities can contribute their own perspectives on how AI should interact with human societies.

Why Is Cultural Wisdom Being Connected to AI?

The initiative is based on the idea that technological systems do not operate independently of society.

AI systems can influence decisions concerning areas such as:

  • Healthcare
  • Agriculture
  • Education
  • Financial services
  • Employment
  • Language and communication
  • Data infrastructure
  • Public services
  • Digital platforms
  • Credit decisions
  • Information access

For example, an algorithm may evaluate a person’s eligibility for a loan, influence the information presented to a child, provide advice to a farmer, translate a local language, or affect decisions made in a workplace.

These applications involve more than technical performance. They can also raise questions about fairness, accountability, dignity, participation, community interests, and who has the authority to make consequential decisions.

The Anima Mundi initiative therefore asks participants to consider what cultural traditions can teach contemporary AI developers about these questions.

As the organisers explain, people who have experienced AI directly already possess important knowledge about its governance. Someone whose loan was assessed by an algorithm, whose agricultural decisions were influenced by an AI system, whose language was translated through technology, or whose work was affected by an automated decision may have valuable insight into how AI should be governed.

The Meaning of “Anima Mundi”

The phrase Anima Mundi is Latin for “the soul of the world.”

The initiative uses the concept to express an understanding of the world as a living and interconnected whole rather than simply as collections of isolated objects or resources.

According to the initiative, this idea recognises that cultures carry different forms of knowledge and meaning through:

  • Stories
  • Ancestral traditions
  • Rivers and natural environments
  • Tools
  • Dance
  • Music
  • Speech
  • Art
  • Community practices

The concept is therefore used as a framework for bringing cultural knowledge into conversations about technology and AI governance.

Connection to the Vatican’s Anima Mundi Collection

The initiative also connects the contemporary AI project to the history of the Vatican’s Anima Mundi collection.

The source explains that a Universal Exposition held in 1925 resulted in approximately one hundred thousand works being brought to Rome from different parts of the world. A permanent ethnological collection subsequently developed from this material.

In 2019, the Vatican reopened the collection under the name Anima Mundi, presenting it as a living space intended to reconnect with the communities from which the cultural works originated.

The initiative draws on this historical idea of cultural reconnection to argue that traditions should not be treated as static or dead artefacts. Instead, they can remain relevant sources of knowledge for contemporary challenges, including AI governance.

Inspired by “Magnifica Humanitas”

The initiative states that it was inspired by Pope Leo XIV’s Magnifica Humanitas and presents two biblical images as a framework for thinking about technology and society.

The Tower of Babel

The first image is the Tower of Babel, which the initiative associates with technology built around:

  • Pride
  • Efficiency
  • Erasure of difference
  • Loss of common language
  • Dispersion and confusion

Within the initiative’s framing, Babel represents a technological approach that fails to sufficiently account for human diversity.

The Rebuilding of Jerusalem

The second image is the rebuilding of Jerusalem under Nehemiah.

This story is presented as an alternative model based on:

  • Shared reconstruction
  • Community participation
  • Collective responsibility
  • Recognition of different contributions
  • Inclusion
  • A commitment that no one is left behind

The initiative uses this contrast to highlight the possibility of treating cultural diversity as a resource for building better approaches to AI governance.

Who Is Being Invited to Participate?

The invitation is deliberately broad.

The initiative initially identifies AI start-ups and industries working in communities as important participants. However, the wider call welcomes submissions from people and organisations around the world.

The organisers specifically invite:

  • Young people
  • Engineers
  • Designers
  • Researchers
  • Founders
  • AI start-ups
  • Industry actors
  • Community members
  • People with lived experience of AI
  • People carrying cultural traditions
  • Participants from African countries
  • Participants from G7 countries
  • Participants from other parts of the world

The initiative particularly encourages young people who are involved in building or studying AI systems, including engineers, designers, researchers, and founders.

Importantly, participants do not have to restrict themselves to the specific mythologies or examples displayed on the initiative’s website. The examples are described as illustrations rather than assignments.

Participants may therefore propose a story, cultural framework, myth, or experience from their own tradition.

Global Participation: Africa and the G7

The initiative brings together communities from the 18 African partner countries of the Italy-Africa Mattei Plan and the G7 countries.

At the same time, participation is not restricted to these geographical areas.

The organisers explicitly state that submissions are welcome from all over the world, while particularly inviting participants from the G7 and the 18 Italy-Africa Mattei Plan partner countries.

The website presents geographical groupings covering:

  1. North Africa
  2. East Africa
  3. West Africa
  4. Central Africa
  5. Southern Africa
  6. G7 countries

The source provided for this opportunity does not enumerate the individual countries within each grouping, so prospective applicants should consult the official initiative for any country-specific clarification.

Click here to start your submission

What Kind of Submission Is Required?

The submission has two principal components:

1. A Digital Artwork

Participants must submit an artwork created in a digital visual medium.

The artwork is not simply intended to illustrate a cultural story independently. The initiative specifically asks for work that has been created in interaction with the machine, with technology functioning as a partner in the creative process.

The technology should therefore contribute to bringing the cultural lesson or insight into contemporary form.

2. A Written Description of Up to 500 Words

Each submission must also include a written description of up to 500 words.

The description can be written in any language of the participant’s choice.

The written submission should identify:

  • The myth, tradition, or cultural frame being used
  • The AI decision or situation being examined
  • Why the myth and AI situation have been paired
  • The difficult or consequential choice involved in the real-world situation

The written description is particularly important because it provides the governance context behind the artistic work.

The AI Decision Must Be Based on a Real-World Situation

One of the most important requirements is that the submission cannot simply describe a hypothetical AI scenario.

Each submission must connect its cultural or mythological frame to a real, named instance involving AI and the private sector.

The initiative identifies six concrete AI moments concerning trust and safety and requires participants to anchor their submissions to an actual situation.

The selected situation must involve:

  • A real start-up or private-sector team
  • An actual community
  • An AI-related decision or interaction
  • A real relationship between the technology provider and the community

The submission should explain what happened and how the relevant decision was made.

What Should the Written Explanation Cover?

The organisers provide a detailed framework for the written description.

Participants are expected to discuss the governance dimension of the AI case alongside the cultural or mythological interpretation.

The write-up should address five major areas.

1. Design or Deployment Choices

Explain what decisions were made when the AI interaction was designed or deployed.

This could involve decisions about how a system interacts with users, what information it uses, what constraints are placed on it, or how a particular AI-enabled service is implemented.

2. Reasons Behind the Decisions

The participant should explain why the relevant decisions were made.

Possible factors identified by the initiative include:

  • Feedback from health workers
  • Internal safety practices
  • Regulation
  • Other forms of organisational or community input

3. People and Organisations Involved

The submission should identify the actors involved in the decision-making process.

These may include:

  • Community partners
  • Government ministries
  • Health ministries
  • Product teams
  • Industry partners
  • Other relevant stakeholders

4. Review and Oversight

The participant should explain how the decision was subsequently:

  • Reviewed
  • Overseen
  • Evaluated
  • Fed back into the AI system or development process

This helps demonstrate that AI governance is an ongoing process rather than a one-time technical decision.

5. Interpretation Through the Cultural Tradition

Finally, the participant should explain what the chosen myth, tradition, or cultural framework makes visible about the AI decision.

The submission should explore:

  • What the tradition helps people notice
  • What questions it raises
  • What assumptions it challenges
  • What lessons it carries forward
  • How it might contribute to thinking about responsible AI

The “Actors, Assets and Actions” Framework

For review purposes, the organisers state that submissions will be read through three questions.

Actors

Who was:

  • Involved?
  • Participating?
  • Responsible?
  • Accountable?

Assets

What exactly was being governed?

This could involve an AI system, data, an interaction, a service, a decision-making process, or another relevant technological asset.

Actions

What was:

  • Done?
  • Allowed?
  • Restricted?
  • Overridden?
  • Left undecided?

The framework also asks how local or cultural wisdom can provide guidance concerning these actions.

Why Communities Are Central to the Initiative

A major principle behind the call is that responsible AI cannot be developed solely through government regulation or private-sector decision-making.

The initiative recognises the important role of governments in building public trust in AI. However, it argues that governments cannot address every dimension of AI governance on their own.

Industry is also presented as an essential stakeholder because companies developing AI tools and solutions have direct knowledge of how these systems are being built, deployed, and experienced.

At the same time, the initiative argues that government and industry together cannot fully provide something that communities possess: long-established moral and cultural traditions concerning what power owes to the people affected by it.

This is why community knowledge and lived experience are placed at the centre of the call.

The Role of Mythology in AI Governance

The initiative’s use of mythology is not simply an artistic exercise.

Instead, mythology is presented as a way of asking questions about contemporary technological decisions.

Traditional stories can contain longstanding reflections on:

  • Power
  • Responsibility
  • Authority
  • Care
  • Reciprocity
  • Domination
  • Dignity
  • Community
  • Human relationships
  • The consequences of decisions

By bringing these stories into conversation with AI, participants can examine technological decisions from perspectives that may not emerge through technical analysis alone.

The purpose is therefore to create a dialogue between ancient or living cultural knowledge and contemporary technological systems.

What Happens to Submitted Works?

The initiative states that all works received will be preserved in a permanent, open online library.

The library is intended to function as a global commons containing traditions and testimonies relating to AI.

This means that the initiative is not simply seeking submissions for a temporary exhibition. The submitted works are intended to contribute to a longer-term collection of cultural perspectives on artificial intelligence.

Click here for more information on Anima Mundi: Global Open Call Invites AI Innovators and Communities to Use Cultural Wisdom to Shape Responsible Artificial Intelligence

Creative Commons Licensing

All submissions are held under Creative Commons licensing and treated as a public good, with attribution to the author.

Applicants should therefore understand that submitting work involves making it available within the initiative’s stated public-good framework while retaining attribution to the creator.

Where and When Is the Initiative Being Presented?

The initiative was announced during the 81st UN General Assembly High Level Week in New York, USA, and at Harmonic Innovation Group’s Words of Hope for a Magnifica Humanitas event in Calabria, Italy, in September 2026.

According to the source, it will also be:

  • Featured in San Francisco in February 2027
  • Presented at the Vatican in September 2027

These events provide additional international platforms for the initiative and its broader conversation about AI, culture, humanity, and governance.

Is There an Application Deadline?

No deadline is stated in the provided opportunity information.

Potential applicants should therefore check the official submission platform and initiative website for any subsequent announcement concerning a closing date, submission window, or updated requirements.

Dialogue Sessions and Additional Engagement

The initiative also provides Dialogue Sessions designed as open question-and-answer spaces and briefings.

Participants and interested members of the public can:

  • Join sessions live
  • Ask questions during the sessions
  • Submit questions in advance
  • Access recordings later

The sessions are recorded and added to the Library, allowing people in different time zones to access them.

Organisations Behind the Initiative

The initiative is associated with the AI Hub for Sustainable Development, alongside MIMIT and UNDP.

The website describes the broader initiative as a G7-endorsed, MIMIT-UNDP co-led initiative focused on accelerating sustainable AI-driven growth with Africa in alignment with the Italy-Africa Mattei Plan.

The named creative and programme leadership includes:

  • Dwayne Carruthers — Creative Co-Director
  • Nicola Campiotti — Creative Co-Director
  • Keyzom Ngodup — Director of the AI Hub for Sustainable Development and Head of Global Digital & AI Programmes, UNDP
  • Henrique Rezende — Coordinator
  • Naveen VarshanIlavarasan — AI Governance Specialist

Why This Opportunity Matters for AI Researchers, Start-ups and Young Innovators

For people working at the intersection of technology, culture, development, governance, and society, the call provides a platform for exploring AI beyond conventional technical discussions.

It creates space to examine questions such as:

  • How should AI systems account for cultural differences?
  • What can traditional knowledge contribute to AI governance?
  • How can communities participate in decisions affecting AI systems?
  • What does responsible AI look like in different cultural contexts?
  • How should developers respond when communities challenge an AI-enabled decision?
  • What forms of knowledge should inform AI safety?
  • How can AI development incorporate local experiences?
  • How can technology contribute to dignity rather than undermine it?
  • How can cultural traditions help identify risks that technical approaches may overlook?

These questions are particularly relevant as AI systems become increasingly embedded in everyday social and economic activities.

Key Submission Requirements at a Glance

Before preparing a submission, prospective participants should ensure that their work addresses the central requirements:

  • Format: Digital visual artwork.
  • Technology: The work must have been made in interaction with a machine.
  • Written component: Maximum 500 words.
  • Language: Any language of the participant’s choice.
  • Cultural component: A myth, cultural tradition, cosmology, story, or lived cultural experience.
  • AI component: A concrete AI decision or interaction.
  • Real-world requirement: The AI case must involve a named real-world start-up or private-sector team and an actual community.
  • Governance component: The submission should explain how the relevant decision was made and governed.
  • Cultural interpretation: Explain what the chosen tradition reveals about the AI decision.
  • Geographical scope: Global.
  • Priority invitations: G7 countries and the 18 Italy-Africa Mattei Plan partner countries.
  • Target participants: Particularly young people, engineers, designers, researchers, founders, start-ups, industries, and people with relevant lived experience.
  • Licensing: Creative Commons, treated as a public good with attribution.
  • Online archive: Submitted works will be preserved in a permanent open online library.
  • Deadline: No deadline is stated in the provided source.

Click here to explore more global AI and Innovation Hub 

Conclusion

The Anima Mundi: The Soul of the World Meets the Machine initiative creates an international platform for connecting cultural knowledge with contemporary debates about artificial intelligence. Rather than treating AI governance solely as a technical or regulatory challenge, the initiative invites participants to examine how mythology, cultural traditions, lived experience, community knowledge, and long-standing ideas about power and responsibility can inform decisions involving AI.

Participants are asked to go beyond abstract discussions by identifying a real-world AI decision involving a private-sector team and an actual community, and then interpreting that situation through a cultural or mythological lens. The resulting digital artwork and written explanation are intended to contribute to a permanent open online library documenting diverse perspectives on AI.

The call is open to participants worldwide, with particular invitations to the G7 and the 18 African partner countries of the Italy-Africa Mattei Plan. Young engineers, designers, researchers, founders, start-ups, industries, and people with direct experience of AI are specifically encouraged to participate.

For anyone interested in artificial intelligence, AI governance, digital transformation, cultural heritage, technology ethics, responsible innovation, community participation, African innovation, or the relationship between technology and society, the initiative offers a distinctive opportunity to place cultural knowledge directly into contemporary conversations about how AI should be developed and governed.

item.content:encoded:
As environmental challenges continue to threaten communities worldwide, the need for informed and empowered young leaders has never been greater. The Council of Europe, through its North-South Centre, is offering young people the opportunity to deepen their understanding of environmental justice, human rights, climate action, and sustainable development through the Human Rights Education for Youth (HEY) Tutored Online Course on Environment.

This fully funded online learning programme equips participants with the knowledge, skills, and advocacy tools needed to address pressing environmental issues such as climate change, biodiversity loss, and pollution through a human rights-based approach. The course is designed to empower young activists, youth leaders, educators, and community advocates from Europe, Africa, and the Middle East to become effective agents of change in their communities.

Why This Course Matters

The world is currently confronted by what experts describe as the “triple planetary crisis”:

  • Climate change
  • Biodiversity loss
  • Pollution

These environmental challenges increasingly affect human dignity, public health, livelihoods, and fundamental freedoms. Access to a clean, healthy, and sustainable environment has become essential for the enjoyment of human rights.

Young people are among the groups most affected by environmental degradation. At the same time, they are leading environmental movements and advocating for stronger protection of natural resources and communities.

Despite this growing engagement, youth-friendly environmental education grounded in human rights remains limited. The HEY Environment Course seeks to bridge this gap by providing practical and accessible education that connects environmental sustainability with human rights protection.

About the HEY Environment Course

The Human Rights Education for Youth (HEY) Environment Course is an intensive online programme organized by the North-South Centre of the Council of Europe.

The programme brings together young people from diverse backgrounds to learn about environmental challenges, legal frameworks, human rights advocacy, and community-based solutions.

Participants will gain a deeper understanding of how environmental degradation impacts vulnerable communities and how young people can actively participate in environmental governance and advocacy.

Course Objectives

The programme aims to achieve several important objectives:

1. Understanding the Triple Planetary Crisis

Participants will explore:

  • Climate change
  • Environmental pollution
  • Biodiversity loss

The course also examines these challenges through a North-South perspective, helping learners understand how environmental issues affect regions differently.

2. Exploring Human Rights and Environmental Connections

Participants will develop a critical understanding of:

  • Human rights principles
  • Environmental justice
  • International legal frameworks
  • Regional environmental agreements
  • Rights-based environmental protection approaches

3. Analysing Impacts on Marginalised Communities

The course examines how environmental degradation disproportionately affects:

  • Vulnerable populations
  • Underrepresented communities
  • Indigenous groups
  • Communities with limited access to environmental resources

Participants will also study community-driven solutions that address environmental and human rights violations.

4. Strengthening Advocacy Skills

A major focus of the programme is empowering young people to:

  • Advocate for environmental justice
  • Promote human rights
  • Organize awareness campaigns
  • Influence decision-making processes
  • Engage in civic participation and policy discussions

Course Structure

The programme is delivered entirely online through the HEY Programme e-learning platform, which is based on Moodle Workplace.

Duration

  • 4 weeks

Learning Modules

The course consists of:

  • Module 1
  • Module 2
  • Module 3
  • Module 4

Participants complete one module each week.

Estimated Workload

  • Approximately 30 hours in total

Learning Methodology

Asynchronous Learning

Participants learn at their own pace and according to their personal schedules.

Collaborative Group Activities

Regular participation in group work is expected. Participants organize and coordinate group activities among themselves.

Live Tutoring Sessions

A limited number of live support sessions will be organized to assist participants throughout the learning process.

Certificate

Participants who successfully complete the programme will receive a Certificate of Participation from the Council of Europe.

Programme Dates

The next edition of the HEY Environment Course will take place:

28 October 2026 to 24 November 2026

Cost and Funding

One of the most attractive aspects of the programme is that participation is completely free.

Benefits

  • No tuition fees
  • Fully online access
  • International learning environment
  • Human rights and environmental education training
  • Networking opportunities with youth leaders from different regions
  • Certificate upon successful completion

Selection Process

A total of 50 participants will be selected for the programme.

Selection will be based primarily on the quality and relevance of the submitted application.

Priority will be given to applicants who:

  • Are active in civil society organisations
  • Participate in youth organizations or youth platforms
  • Work within youth-related institutions
  • Demonstrate the potential to share acquired knowledge with others
  • Show commitment to environmental and human rights issues

Applicants must also have the ability to communicate effectively in English, which serves as the working language of the course.

The selection process will be conducted jointly by the North-South Centre of the Council of Europe and its partner organizations.

The Council of Europe welcomes applications from all eligible candidates regardless of:

  • Gender
  • Disability
  • Marital status
  • Parental status
  • Racial background
  • Ethnic origin
  • Social origin
  • Religion
  • Belief
  • Sexual orientation

Connection with the iLEGEND III Programme

The HEY Environment Course forms part of the iLEGEND III project (Intercultural Learning Exchange through Global Education, Networking and Dialogue 2022-2026).

This initiative is a joint programme of:

  • The European Union
  • The Council of Europe

The project seeks to encourage active youth participation in addressing global challenges, promoting sustainable development, and reducing inequalities at both local and international levels.

Through this broader initiative, participants become part of a larger movement that promotes intercultural dialogue, democratic participation, and global citizenship.

Partner Organisations

The programme is supported by respected international institutions, including:

  • UNEP (United Nations Environment Programme)
  • UNESCO-UV Chair for Global Education in the Mediterranean

These partnerships contribute expertise in environmental education, sustainability, and global citizenship.

Deadline for Applications

18 October 2026 at 23:59 UTC/GMT+1 (Lisbon Time)

Selection Results Announcement

23 October 2026

Applicants should note that only selected candidates will be contacted due to the large number of expected applications.

Selected participants must confirm their participation within the specified timeframe after receiving their selection notification.

Qualifications

  • Must be 30 years old or younger
  • Must demonstrate interest in environmental and human rights issues
  • Must be active in civil society, youth work, activism, education, advocacy, media, policymaking, or related fields
  • Must possess sufficient English-language communication skills
  • Must be willing to participate throughout the 4-week course
  • Should have potential to disseminate knowledge gained through the course

Eligible Countries and Regions

Applicants can apply from:

  • The 46 Council of Europe Member States
  • African countries
  • Countries in the Middle East

Race Eligibility

  • All races and ethnic backgrounds are eligible.
  • The programme explicitly encourages diversity and non-discrimination in its selection process.

APPLY HERE:

Click here for more information on this opportunity: 

Conclusion

The Council of Europe HEY Environment Course 2026 presents an exceptional opportunity for young people passionate about environmental protection, human rights, climate justice, and sustainable development. Through its comprehensive curriculum, international network, expert guidance, and fully funded online format, the programme empowers future leaders to understand the complex relationship between environmental challenges and human rights.

For aspiring youth advocates, educators, activists, community leaders, and environmental defenders, this course offers both the knowledge and practical tools necessary to create meaningful change. As the world faces growing environmental crises, strengthening the capacity of young people to lead sustainable and rights-based solutions remains a critical investment in our collective future.

item.content:encoded:
The American Political Science Association (APSA) Diversity Fellowship Program (DFP) 2027–2028 Fall Cycle is now accepting applications from emerging scholars who are preparing to pursue doctoral study in political science and whose academic interests engage with important questions concerning race, ethnicity, gender, systemic racism, LGBTQ politics, disability politics, Indigenous politics, or tribal sovereignty and governance.

The fellowship is designed to support prospective political scientists as they move toward doctoral-level study and develop careers involving political science research, scholarship, and teaching.

For the 2027–2028 fellowship cycle, successful fellows will receive $5,000, disbursed over two years. The Fall Cycle application deadline is October 25, 2026.

About the APSA Diversity Fellowship Program

The American Political Science Association (APSA) established its Diversity Fellowship Program as part of its broader diversity and inclusion efforts within the political science profession.

The program is particularly relevant to students and emerging scholars who are preparing to enter PhD programs in political science and whose prospective research connects with areas that have historically been important to scholarship on inequality, representation, identity, governance, political participation, discrimination, and the experiences of historically underrepresented communities.

The 2027–2028 Fall Cycle is specifically open to individuals who are undergraduate seniors, recent graduates, students in terminal MA programs, or other individuals currently in the process of applying to PhD programs in political science.

The fellowship provides financial support while also recognizing applicants’ potential to contribute to political science through future research and teaching.

Fellowship Award: $5,000

One of the key features of the 2027–2028 APSA Diversity Fellowship is the financial award.

Selected fellows will receive $5,000, distributed over two years.

For prospective doctoral students, financial support at the pre-PhD or PhD-application stage can help reduce some of the financial pressures associated with preparing for graduate study and developing an academic career.

Applicants should, however, carefully review the official APSA application information for the full terms and conditions associated with the fellowship.

Who Should Consider Applying?

The fellowship is particularly relevant to students and emerging scholars who are preparing for doctoral study in political science and whose research interests fall within the program’s specified areas.

Eligible applicants may include:

  1. Undergraduate seniors preparing to apply for political science PhD programs.
  2. Recent graduates who are preparing for doctoral study.
  3. Students enrolled in terminal MA programs who are applying to PhD programs in political science.
  4. Other prospective PhD applicants who satisfy the program’s eligibility requirements.

The important distinction is that the Fall Cycle is aimed at individuals who are in the process of applying for PhD programs in political science, rather than applicants who are simply seeking general graduate funding.

Research Areas Covered by the Fellowship

A central requirement of the APSA Diversity Fellowship Program is the applicant’s research or intended scholarship.

Fall Cycle applicants must be engaged in, or planning to pursue, political science research and scholarship primarily focused on one or more of the following areas:

  • Race
  • Ethnicity
  • Gender
  • Systemic racism
  • LGBTQ politics
  • Disability politics
  • Indigenous politics
  • Tribal sovereignty and governance

These areas encompass a wide range of political science research questions.

For example, prospective applicants may investigate questions concerning political representation, political institutions, public policy, governance, political participation, social movements, discrimination, identity, state–community relationships, Indigenous governance, or the political experiences of marginalized populations, provided that the proposed research fits the program’s stated focus.

Applicants should ensure that their proposed research is genuinely situated within political science and aligns substantially with the fellowship’s specified areas of interest.

Teaching and Research Potential

The APSA Diversity Fellowship is not solely concerned with an applicant’s research topic.

Applicants must also be able to demonstrate an interest in teaching and potential for research in political science.

This means that prospective applicants should be prepared to communicate how their academic trajectory could contribute to political science as a discipline.

When preparing an application, applicants may therefore wish to clearly articulate:

  • Their academic background
  • Their research interests
  • Their proposed area of doctoral study
  • Their interest in political science
  • Their long-term research objectives
  • Their interest in teaching
  • How their academic experiences have prepared them for doctoral study
  • How their proposed scholarship connects to the fellowship’s research areas

A strong application should present a coherent connection between the applicant’s previous academic preparation, proposed doctoral research, and future contribution to political science.

First-Generation and Historically Underrepresented Scholars

APSA states that first-generation students and scholars are strongly encouraged to apply.

The organization also specifically encourages individuals from historically underrepresented racial and ethnic groups, including:

  • African Americans
  • Asian and Asian Pacific Americans
  • Latinos/as
  • American Indians or Alaska Natives
  • Native Hawaiians
  • Scholars of MENA descent

These groups are identified by APSA as communities that have historically been underrepresented in the political science profession.

It is important to distinguish between being strongly encouraged to apply and satisfying the program’s formal eligibility requirements. Applicants must still meet the fellowship’s applicable citizenship or immigration-status and academic requirements.

U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Requirements

A particularly important part of the Fall Cycle eligibility criteria concerns citizenship and immigration status.

At the time of application, an applicant must be:

  • A U.S. citizen;
  • A U.S. national;
  • A U.S. permanent resident, meaning a holder of a Permanent Resident Card; or
  • An individual who has been granted Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) status.

This requirement means that the fellowship is not a general international fellowship open to prospective political science PhD students worldwide.

For example, simply being an international student interested in pursuing a PhD in political science in the United States does not, by itself, satisfy the stated citizenship or immigration requirement.

Prospective international applicants should therefore verify their status against APSA’s official criteria before investing significant time in preparing an application.

Application Deadline

The deadline for the 2027–2028 APSA Diversity Fellowship Program Fall Cycle is October 25, 2026.

Important Deadline

October 25, 2026

Applicants should not wait until the final day to begin preparing their application because the program requires multiple components, including transcripts and three recommendation letters.

In particular, applicants should allow sufficient time for their recommenders to prepare and submit their letters directly through the application system.

To apply, create an APSA profile here  and submit your online application here

Application Requirements

The Fall Cycle application consists of several important components.

1. Online Application

Applicants must complete the APSA online application.

The application includes fields for:

  • Personal statement
  • Resume
  • List of recommenders

The application is submitted through the APSA application system.

Applicants should ensure that the information presented across the application is consistent and clearly communicates their academic background, research interests, doctoral ambitions, and suitability for the fellowship.

2. Academic Transcripts

Applicants must upload academic records from each undergraduate and graduate institution attended.

APSA states that applicants may submit:

  • Official transcripts
  • Unofficial transcripts
  • Degree audits

for application review.

Applicants should therefore gather records from all relevant institutions well before the application deadline.

3. Three Letters of Recommendation

Applicants must obtain three letters of recommendation.

Importantly, the letters are not simply uploaded by the applicant. Recommenders must submit their letters directly to the application system.

Applicants will be prompted to send recommendation requests through the application.

Because recommendation letters require action from third parties, prospective applicants should contact their recommenders well ahead of the October 25, 2026 deadline.

Recommended Application Preparation

Although applicants should follow APSA’s official requirements rather than relying on informal application advice, prospective candidates can organize their preparation around several practical steps.

Step 1: Confirm Eligibility

Before preparing the full application, verify that you satisfy the fellowship’s requirements concerning:

  • Academic stage
  • PhD application status
  • Political science research interests
  • Citizenship or immigration status
  • Interest in teaching and political science research

This is particularly important because the program has specific eligibility requirements rather than being an unrestricted graduate scholarship.

Step 2: Clarify Your Research Direction

Your research interests should be clearly connected to the fellowship’s stated areas.

Consider how your proposed doctoral research relates to questions involving:

  • Race
  • Ethnicity
  • Gender
  • Systemic racism
  • LGBTQ politics
  • Disability politics
  • Indigenous politics
  • Tribal sovereignty and governance

The connection should be substantive rather than simply mentioning one of these subjects in passing.

Step 3: Prepare Your Personal Statement

The personal statement provides an opportunity to explain your academic trajectory and future goals.

Applicants should aim to present a coherent narrative covering their:

  • Academic preparation
  • Research interests
  • Motivation for pursuing political science
  • Proposed doctoral direction
  • Interest in teaching
  • Long-term scholarly objectives

The statement should also make the relationship between the applicant’s research interests and the Diversity Fellowship Program clear.

Step 4: Update Your Resume

The application requires a resume.

Applicants should ensure that their resume accurately presents relevant:

  • Educational qualifications
  • Research experience
  • Publications, where applicable
  • Conference participation
  • Teaching experience
  • Academic projects
  • Research skills
  • Awards and distinctions
  • Professional or service experience relevant to political science

The resume should complement rather than simply repeat the personal statement.

Step 5: Contact Three Recommenders

Applicants should identify three individuals who can provide substantive recommendations and contact them early.

Since recommenders submit their letters directly through the application system, applicants should not assume that completing their own application automatically completes the recommendation requirement.

Step 6: Gather Transcripts

Collect transcripts or degree audits from every undergraduate and graduate institution attended.

Having these documents ready before beginning the final submission process can reduce delays.

Key Facts at a Glance

Item Details
Opportunity APSA Diversity Fellowship Program
Cycle 2027–2028 Fall Cycle
Category Fellowship
Award $5,000
Payment period Disbursed over two years
Application deadline October 25, 2026

Intended doctoral field Political Science
Research focus Race, ethnicity, gender, systemic racism, LGBTQ politics, disability politics, Indigenous politics, tribal sovereignty and governance
Teaching requirement Applicants must demonstrate an interest in teaching
Research requirement Applicants must demonstrate potential for research in political science
Recommendation letters Three
Transcripts Required from each undergraduate and graduate institution attended

Nationality/status requirement U.S. citizen, U.S. national, U.S. permanent resident, or DACA recipient

The details above reflect APSA’s published information for the 2027–2028 Fall Cycle.

Why Prospective PhD Applicants Should Pay Attention to the Deadline

The October 25, 2026 deadline is especially important because this application involves materials that cannot necessarily be completed at the last minute.

In addition to the applicant’s own personal statement and resume, the application requires academic records and three recommendation letters. Since recommenders must submit their letters directly through the application system, applicants should begin the process sufficiently early to allow their recommenders to complete their submissions.

Applicants should also take time to ensure that their proposed research is genuinely aligned with the fellowship’s areas of focus and that their application presents a clear trajectory toward doctoral study and a career involving political science research and teaching.

Click here for frequently asked questions 

Conclusion

The 2027–2028 APSA Diversity Fellowship Program Fall Cycle provides a $5,000 fellowship distributed over two years for eligible emerging scholars preparing to pursue PhD study in political science. The program is particularly focused on applicants whose prospective research engages with race, ethnicity, gender, systemic racism, LGBTQ politics, disability politics, Indigenous politics, or tribal sovereignty and governance.

Prospective applicants should pay particular attention to the program’s U.S. citizenship and immigration-status requirements, its requirement that applicants be pursuing or preparing for a PhD in political science, and its expectation that applicants demonstrate an interest in both teaching and political science research.

The application requires a personal statement, resume, transcripts or degree audits from all relevant institutions, and three recommendation letters submitted directly by recommenders.

Most importantly, the application deadline is October 25, 2026. Prospective applicants should therefore begin preparing their materials and contacting recommenders well before the deadline.

item.content:encoded:
The MAXMINDS 2.0 Max Planck Initiative for Researchers At-Risk is a mentorship programme supporting researchers whose academic and research careers have been disrupted or threatened by war or natural disasters. The initiative connects eligible researchers with mentors from the Max Planck research community who can provide personalised guidance, professional connections and support in navigating academic and research opportunities.

The programme is open to researchers at Master’s level and above, across different career stages and regardless of nationality. For the 2026/27 programme, applications are open until 18 October 2026 at 23:59 CEST.

MAXMINDS 2.0 is a mentorship initiative rather than a direct funding programme. Its purpose is to help researchers facing difficult circumstances identify opportunities, strengthen applications and rebuild their academic and professional networks.

What Is MAXMINDS 2.0?

MAXMINDS 2.0, the Max Planck Initiative for Researchers At-Risk, was established to support researchers who are facing acute threats to their academic careers because of displacement, particularly in situations involving war or natural disasters.

Displacement can interrupt research projects, separate researchers from universities and research groups, restrict access to laboratories and academic resources, and make it difficult to maintain professional networks. Researchers may also struggle to find information about fellowships, scholarships, research stays or positions that could help them continue their careers.

MAXMINDS 2.0 responds to these challenges by providing a structured mentoring relationship. Eligible researchers are matched with mentors whose expertise and research interests can be relevant to their academic background and future goals.

Through this relationship, mentees can receive practical advice while exploring opportunities within the Max Planck Society and the wider research environment.

Who Can Apply for MAXMINDS 2.0?

The programme is intended for researchers who meet both the academic and displacement-related requirements.

Applicants should:

  • Be at Master’s level or above.
  • Be in acute danger of displacement by war or have been recently displaced by war or a natural disaster.
  • Have limited access to research resources and institutional support.
  • Be seeking to continue or develop their academic or research career.
  • Be willing to participate in a structured mentoring relationship.

MAXMINDS 2.0 is open to all nationalities. It is also not restricted to one particular academic discipline or career stage. Eligible applicants may include Master’s students, doctoral researchers, early-career researchers, mid-career researchers and senior researchers, provided they meet the programme’s core requirements.

What Does the Programme Offer?

MAXMINDS 2.0 provides individualised support designed around the needs and research interests of each mentee.

Mentorship and Career Guidance

Participants are connected with experienced researchers who can offer advice on academic and research-career development. Mentors and mentees work together to identify useful opportunities and determine practical steps towards the mentee’s goals.

Application and CV Support

Mentors can provide guidance on applications for internships, scholarships, fellowships, research stays and research positions. They can also advise mentees on presenting their academic experience, research interests and professional background effectively in applications and CVs.

Professional Connections

Researchers affected by displacement may have lost access to established academic networks. MAXMINDS 2.0 can help participants develop professional connections through their mentoring relationship and the wider research community.

Information on Research Opportunities

The initiative also serves as a source of information about fellowships and other research opportunities. Its broader opportunities platform includes resources relevant to researchers at different career stages, including mid-career and senior researchers.

How Does the Mentoring Programme Work?

Once applications have been reviewed, successful participants go through an onboarding and mentor-matching process.

The matching process considers the research interests and expertise of mentors and mentees so that the relationship can provide meaningful academic and professional guidance.

The fast-track mentoring programme involves regular meetings between the mentor and mentee. The programme information indicates that participants should have at least four meetings during the initial mentoring period, with the possibility of extending the relationship to at least six meetings by mutual agreement.

For the 2026/27 round, the main mentoring period is scheduled for November 2026 to March 2027.

Mentors and mentees are also expected to follow the MAXMINDS 2.0 Code of Conduct, which establishes expectations for the mentoring relationship.

Is MAXMINDS 2.0 Fully Funded?

No. MAXMINDS 2.0 does not currently provide direct financial funding to participants.

This is an important distinction for applicants. The programme provides mentorship and guidance that can help researchers pursue other opportunities, including scholarships, fellowships, internships, research stays and positions.

Participation therefore does not automatically result in a scholarship, research position, fellowship or financial award. Instead, the programme helps researchers navigate these opportunities with support from an experienced mentor.

2026/27 MAXMINDS 2.0 Timeline

The programme follows the schedule below:

Stage Date
Application deadline 18 October 2026, 23:59 CEST
Selection End of October 2026
Applicants notified By 30 October 2026
Onboarding and mentor matching November 2026
Mentoring November 2026 – March 2027

Applicants should submit their forms before the deadline and ensure that the information provided accurately reflects their academic background and circumstances.

How to Apply for MAXMINDS 2.0

The application process is completed online through the official MAXMINDS 2.0 application form.

1. Review the Eligibility Requirements

Before applying, make sure you meet the programme’s Master’s-level-or-above requirement and the criteria relating to displacement and access to research resources and institutional support.

2. Prepare Your Information

Applicants should be ready to provide relevant information about their academic background, research experience, research interests and current circumstances.

3. Explain Your Research and Career Needs

Since the programme is based on individual mentorship, applicants should clearly communicate the type of academic or research support they need and the opportunities they hope to pursue.

4. Submit the Online Form

Complete and submit the official MAXMINDS 2.0 application form before 18 October 2026 at 23:59 CEST.

According to the programme timeline, applications will be reviewed towards the end of October, with successful applicants moving into onboarding and mentor matching in November.

Important Details at a Glance

Programme: MAXMINDS 2.0 – Max Planck Initiative for Researchers At-Risk
Organisation: Max Planck Society
Opportunity type: Research mentorship and career support
Academic level: Master’s level and above
Career stages: All career levels, subject to eligibility requirements
Nationality: Open regardless of nationality
Target group: Researchers at risk of displacement or recently displaced by war or natural disasters
Support: Mentorship, application and CV guidance, professional connections and research-opportunity information
Direct funding: Not currently provided
Mentoring period: November 2026 – March 2027
Application deadline: 18 October 2026 at 23:59 CEST

Application Portal

Researchers interested in MAXMINDS 2.0 should apply through the official online application form.

Access Application Form Here

Official Programme Information

 

The MAXMINDS 2.0 Max Planck Initiative for Researchers At-Risk offers structured mentorship to researchers whose academic careers have been affected or threatened by war or natural disasters. By connecting eligible researchers with experienced mentors, the programme provides practical support with applications, CVs, professional networking and navigating further research opportunities.

The initiative is open to eligible researchers from the Master’s level onward, regardless of nationality or career stage. While MAXMINDS 2.0 does not provide direct funding, its mentorship can help participants identify and pursue scholarships, fellowships, internships, research stays and other academic opportunities.

Applications for the 2026/27 programme close on 18 October 2026 at 23:59 CEST.

item.content:encoded:
The Crisis Leadership Summits for Preparedness bring Harvard-trained crisis leadership education directly into local communities, creating an opportunity for leaders from government, business, nonprofit organizations, public safety, public health, faith-based organizations, human services, and other sectors to prepare collectively for increasingly complex emergencies.

Convened within participating communities and taught by Harvard NPLI faculty and experienced crisis leaders, these 1–1.5-day summits are designed around the reality that effective disaster preparedness cannot depend on a single institution or sector. Modern crises often cross organizational, geographic, and professional boundaries. Communities therefore need leaders who can communicate across sectors, understand interconnected systems, coordinate under pressure, and work toward a unified response.

The initiative is accepting applications for 2026 and 2027, allowing communities to bring the training to their own local networks and develop stronger preparedness relationships before an emergency occurs.

What Are Crisis Leadership Summits for Preparedness?

The Crisis Leadership Summit is a community-based leadership training seminar developed through the National Preparedness Leadership Initiative (NPLI) at Harvard.

The program is built around the concept of Meta-Leadership, a leadership approach developed through more than two decades of research, teaching, and practical experience in crisis preparedness and response. Rather than focusing only on the responsibilities of a single organization, Meta-Leadership emphasizes the ability to understand the wider system, connect different organizations, and coordinate leadership across institutional and sectoral boundaries.

The Summit brings together leaders who may have different responsibilities during a crisis but whose decisions and actions are interconnected.

Participants can include representatives from:

  • Government and local authorities
  • Public safety and emergency management
  • Public health organizations
  • Hospitals and healthcare institutions
  • Local nonprofit organizations
  • Human service organizations
  • Businesses and private-sector organizations
  • Faith-based organizations
  • Community organizations
  • Educational institutions
  • Political and civic leadership
  • Other organizations involved in community preparedness and crisis response

The central objective is to help these leaders establish relationships and a shared leadership framework before an emergency occurs, rather than attempting to build coordination for the first time during a disaster.

Bring Harvard NPLI Faculty and Crisis Leadership Training to Your Community

One of the defining features of the program is that the Summit is convened within the community itself.

Rather than requiring every local leader to travel to a distant training center, participating communities can bring Harvard NPLI faculty and experienced crisis leaders into their own community.

This allows the Summit to focus on the specific characteristics, institutions, vulnerabilities, and risks of the participating community.

The training includes:

  • Harvard-developed Meta-Leadership concepts and practices
  • Practical crisis leadership tools
  • Cross-sector leadership development
  • Community preparedness discussions
  • Crisis response and recovery considerations
  • Customized crisis simulations
  • Networking between local leaders
  • Shared approaches to crisis communication and coordination
  • Systems thinking and decision-making exercises
  • Lessons derived from extensive crisis leadership research and practice

The result is intended to be more than a one-day training event. The Summit is designed as a launch point for continuing community connectivity and preparedness.

 

Why Cross-Sector Crisis Leadership Matters

Disasters rarely affect only one organization.

A major flood, wildfire, pandemic, cyber incident, infrastructure failure, public health emergency, extreme weather event, or other crisis can simultaneously affect government services, businesses, healthcare systems, schools, transportation, community organizations, families, and vulnerable populations.

For example, during a major disaster:

  1. Government agencies may coordinate emergency management and public services.
  2. Public safety organizations may manage immediate response and evacuation.
  3. Healthcare institutions may face increased demand for emergency and medical services.
  4. Businesses may need to maintain critical services and supply chains.
  5. Nonprofits and community organizations may provide food, shelter, financial assistance, or other support.
  6. Faith-based organizations may assist with community outreach and emergency support.
  7. Human service organizations may work with populations facing heightened vulnerability.
  8. Political and civic leaders may communicate with the public and coordinate community-level action.

These responsibilities are interconnected.

A breakdown in communication between organizations can create delays, duplication of efforts, gaps in services, or confusion over responsibilities.

The Crisis Leadership Summit therefore focuses on strengthening relationships before a crisis happens.

The underlying principle is simple: communities should know who they need to work with before they need to work together under emergency conditions.

Understanding Meta-Leadership

The Crisis Leadership Summit curriculum is based on Meta-Leadership, a framework developed through extensive research, practice, and teaching at Harvard.

Meta-Leadership focuses on leadership beyond the boundaries of a single organization.

Instead of asking only:

“How can my organization respond?”

leaders are encouraged to consider broader questions such as:

  • What is happening across the entire system?
  • Which organizations and leaders are affected?
  • What information does each sector possess?
  • Where are the dependencies between organizations?
  • How can leaders coordinate their actions?
  • How can organizations communicate effectively during uncertainty?
  • Where are potential gaps in the response?
  • How can leaders work collectively toward a common objective?

This systems-oriented approach is particularly relevant to complex emergencies where no single organization possesses all the information, resources, authority, or capabilities required to address the situation independently.

Customized Crisis Simulations

A major component of the Summit is its use of customized crisis simulations.

Rather than relying exclusively on theoretical discussion, the program can incorporate simulations designed around the participating community’s unique risk profile.

This provides leaders with an opportunity to explore how they might respond when confronted with a rapidly evolving crisis.

A community’s simulation could be informed by risks relevant to its particular context, such as:

  • Natural disasters
  • Extreme weather
  • Public health emergencies
  • Infrastructure disruption
  • Community safety challenges
  • Supply-chain disruption
  • Major emergencies affecting essential services
  • Complex events requiring coordination between multiple organizations

The simulations are intended to help participants practice leadership and coordination in conditions where information may be incomplete, circumstances may change rapidly, and multiple organizations must act simultaneously.

What Participants Can Gain From the Summit

The program is designed to strengthen both individual leadership capabilities and broader community preparedness.

  1. Stronger Cross-Sector Collaboration

Participants have the opportunity to meet leaders from sectors that they may need to work with during an emergency.

Building these relationships in advance can help establish communication channels and familiarity between organizations.

The program’s approach can be summarized by the idea of exchanging business cards before an emergency, rather than attempting to identify key partners for the first time in the middle of a crisis.

  1. A Shared Crisis Leadership Framework

Different organizations often use different terminology, procedures, priorities, and decision-making structures.

The Summit introduces a shared leadership vocabulary and framework that can help participating leaders communicate more effectively across organizational boundaries.

  1. Practical Leadership Tools

The program focuses on pragmatic tools that leaders can use when navigating:

  • Crisis disruption
  • Emergency response
  • Uncertainty
  • Recovery
  • Complex decision-making
  • Cross-organizational coordination
  • Communication challenges

The objective is to provide approaches that can be applied during emergencies as well as in everyday leadership situations.

  1. Systems Thinking

Complex crises require leaders to understand how different parts of a community interact.

Systems thinking encourages participants to look beyond their own organization and consider the wider network of institutions, people, resources, risks, and dependencies involved in a crisis.

This can support more coordinated decision-making and help leaders identify potential gaps before an emergency occurs.

  1. Greater Community Resilience

Preparedness is not solely about emergency response plans.

It also involves relationships, leadership capacity, institutional coordination, information sharing, and community networks.

By bringing leaders together, the Summit seeks to strengthen the broader ecosystem that supports community resilience.

  1. Improved Crisis Decision-Making

During a crisis, leaders may have to make important decisions despite uncertainty and rapidly changing circumstances.

The Summit provides participants with frameworks and practical exercises intended to strengthen decision-making before, during, and after crises.

  1. Stronger Coordination During Response and Recovery

The leadership relationships developed during the Summit can provide a foundation for continued cooperation.

This can be particularly important when recovery requires coordination between public agencies, private organizations, nonprofits, healthcare institutions, and community groups.

Benefits for the Community

The value of the Summit extends beyond individual participants.

A successful preparedness program can contribute to a more connected local leadership network.

Potential community-level benefits include:

  • Stronger relationships between government and non-government organizations
  • Better understanding of local crisis-response responsibilities
  • Greater awareness of organizational capabilities and limitations
  • Improved communication across sectors
  • More coordinated emergency leadership
  • Greater preparedness for complex and evolving crises
  • Stronger community resilience
  • Continued collaboration following the Summit
  • Improved capacity to navigate disruption and recovery

The Summit is therefore positioned as a starting point for a broader preparedness network rather than simply a standalone educational seminar.

Impact in Action: Springfield, Missouri Summit

The program highlights the Springfield, Missouri Crisis Leadership Summit, held in October 2025, as an example of the initiative’s community-level reach.

The reported figures include:

  • 316 cross-sector community leaders
  • 65 organizations represented
  • 4 customized crisis simulations

These figures demonstrate the scale at which a community-based crisis leadership program can convene leaders from different sectors around preparedness and coordinated response.

The Springfield Summit provides an example of how the model can bring together a broad network of organizations and use customized simulations to explore crisis leadership within a specific local context.

Summit Curriculum

The Crisis Leadership Summit curriculum combines leadership education, practical exercises, community engagement, and crisis simulations.

The curriculum includes several interconnected components.

Crisis Leadership Education

Participants are introduced to the principles and practices of Meta-Leadership and how they can be applied to complex emergencies.

Crisis Simulations

Customized scenarios provide participants with an opportunity to apply leadership concepts to realistic crisis situations.

Community-Specific Preparedness

The Summit considers the particular risk environment and organizational landscape of the participating community.

Cross-Sector Networking

Participants interact with leaders from different sectors, creating opportunities to establish relationships and understand the capabilities of other organizations.

Practical Leadership Application

The program emphasizes tools and frameworks that participants can apply beyond the training environment.

Sample Preparedness Summit Agenda

A typical Summit can combine several different formats rather than relying exclusively on lectures.

Depending on the community and program design, activities may include:

  1. Opening and introduction to the Summit
  2. Introduction to crisis leadership and Meta-Leadership
  3. Cross-sector leadership discussions
  4. Exploration of community preparedness challenges
  5. Leadership tools and practical frameworks
  6. Crisis simulation exercises
  7. Facilitated discussion and reflection
  8. Cross-sector networking
  9. Application of lessons to local preparedness
  10. Discussion of continued community collaboration

The precise structure can be tailored to the participating community and its preparedness needs.

Who Can Benefit From Participating?

The Summit is particularly relevant to communities seeking to strengthen relationships among leaders responsible for preparedness, response, public services, business continuity, healthcare, social support, and community resilience.

Potential participants can come from a wide range of sectors, including:

Government and Public Administration

Local government officials, public administrators, emergency management professionals, and other public-sector leaders can use the Summit to strengthen coordination with organizations outside government.

Public Safety

Police, fire, emergency management, and other public safety professionals can benefit from stronger relationships with organizations that provide essential services during emergencies.

Public Health and Healthcare

Public health departments, hospitals, healthcare organizations, and health-sector leaders play a critical role in responding to emergencies that affect community health and wellbeing.

Nonprofit and Human Services Organizations

Nonprofits and human service organizations often work directly with communities and populations requiring assistance during emergencies.

Businesses

Private-sector organizations can play an important role in maintaining essential services, supporting employees and communities, and sustaining economic activity during disruptions.

Faith-Based Organizations

Faith-based organizations can serve as established community networks and may play important roles in outreach, communication, shelter, and community support.

Civic and Political Leadership

Civic and political leaders can contribute to community communication, coordination, decision-making, and public engagement during emergencies.

Why Preparedness Needs to Begin Before a Crisis

One of the central ideas behind the Crisis Leadership Summit is that effective crisis leadership should not begin when the emergency begins.

By the time a major disaster occurs, organizations may already be operating under intense pressure.

Leaders may be dealing with:

  • Limited information
  • Rapidly changing circumstances
  • High public expectations
  • Resource constraints
  • Communication challenges
  • Multiple competing priorities
  • Increased demand for services
  • Interdependencies between organizations

Establishing relationships before these pressures emerge can create a stronger foundation for coordination.

Preparedness therefore involves not only plans and infrastructure but also people, relationships, leadership practices, communication, and trust.

A Community-Based Approach to Resilience

The Summit’s community-based format recognizes that preparedness is highly dependent on local conditions.

Every community has a different combination of:

  • Geographic characteristics
  • Infrastructure
  • Population needs
  • Economic conditions
  • Public institutions
  • Healthcare capacity
  • Emergency-response organizations
  • Community networks
  • Environmental risks
  • Critical services

A standardized crisis-response model may therefore need to be complemented by locally informed leadership preparation.

Customized simulations provide a mechanism for exploring how leadership coordination could function under the particular conditions of a participating community.

Partnering With NPLI at Harvard

Communities interested in organizing a Crisis Leadership Summit can explore opportunities to partner with the National Preparedness Leadership Initiative at Harvard.

The program brings together Harvard NPLI faculty and experienced crisis leaders to deliver the Summit within the participating community.

The partnership model is intended to connect Harvard’s crisis leadership research and teaching with local preparedness networks.

Through this approach, communities can combine external expertise with knowledge of their own local institutions, risks, resources, and leadership networks.

History and the Current Summit Initiative

The Crisis Leadership Summit initiative builds on the broader work of the National Preparedness Leadership Initiative and its development of Meta-Leadership through research, teaching, and practical crisis leadership experience.

The current initiative provides communities with a way to translate this body of work into locally focused preparedness training.

Its emphasis on cross-sector leadership reflects the increasingly interconnected nature of modern emergencies.

A crisis affecting one part of a community can rapidly create consequences for multiple sectors. Effective preparedness therefore requires leaders to understand not only their own responsibilities but also how their actions connect with those of other organizations.

Program Details at a Glance

Program Feature Details
Program Crisis Leadership Summits for Preparedness
Format Convened within the participating community
Duration 1–1.5 days
Availability 2026 and 2027
Participants Local cross-sector leaders
Faculty Harvard NPLI Faculty and experienced crisis leaders
Core Framework Meta-Leadership
Key Training Element Customized crisis simulations
Focus Preparedness, crisis leadership, collaboration, response and recovery
Community Objective Build a stronger cross-sector leadership network

Click here to apply

Crisis Leadership Program Application – NPLI

 

What Makes the Program Community-Focused?

The Summit does not treat preparedness as the responsibility of one institution.

Instead, it recognizes the importance of creating connections among the organizations that collectively make up a community’s crisis-response ecosystem.

A community may have excellent emergency-management personnel, healthcare professionals, nonprofits, businesses, public safety agencies, and government officials. However, preparedness can be strengthened when these leaders understand one another’s roles and establish communication pathways before an emergency occurs.

This cross-sector approach is one of the central features of the program.

 

From Training to Long-Term Preparedness

The Summit is designed to serve as a launch point for continued community connectivity.

The training itself lasts approximately 1–1.5 days, but the relationships developed during the program can potentially support longer-term collaboration.

Following the Summit, participating leaders can continue to:

  • Maintain cross-sector relationships
  • Share preparedness information
  • Identify emerging risks
  • Coordinate preparedness initiatives
  • Exchange lessons learned
  • Strengthen organizational connections
  • Continue conversations around community resilience
  • Improve understanding of each sector’s capabilities

This longer-term connectivity is particularly important because preparedness is an ongoing process rather than a one-time activity.

Click here for more information 

 

Conclusion

The Crisis Leadership Summits for Preparedness provide a community-based approach to strengthening crisis leadership, preparedness, and cross-sector collaboration. Through Harvard NPLI faculty, Meta-Leadership education, practical leadership tools, networking, systems thinking, and customized crisis simulations, the program brings together leaders who may be called upon to work together during complex emergencies.

With Summits available for 2026 and 2027 and a format designed to be convened directly within communities, the initiative provides a framework for connecting government, business, nonprofit, public safety, public health, faith-based, human service, and civic leaders before a crisis occurs.

The broader objective is to build communities in which leaders are not meeting for the first time during an emergency, but already have relationships, shared language, an understanding of their interconnected responsibilities, and practical tools for navigating disruption.

For communities seeking to strengthen preparedness and develop a more connected network of crisis leaders, the Summit offers a structured opportunity to bring Harvard NPLI’s crisis leadership education directly into the local context.
