item.content:encoded:
The Canadian Institutes of Health Research (CIHR) has opened the 2027 Health System Impact Fellowship (HSI Fellowship), a major research and professional development opportunity designed for highly qualified doctoral trainees and post-doctoral researchers working in health services and policy research (HSPR) and related fields.

The fellowship provides researchers with an opportunity to move beyond the traditional university research environment and work directly within health system organizations on research projects addressing real-world health system challenges. Through this embedded research model, fellows can apply their research, analytical and professional skills to issues affecting health services, health policy, public health and health system performance.

The 2027 competition offers two streams: a one-year fellowship for doctoral trainees and a two-year fellowship for post-doctoral researchers. Successful applicants can receive funding of up to $50,000 for the doctoral stream or $155,000 for the post-doctoral stream, including stipends and professional development and research allowances.

The application deadline for the 2027 competition is January 12, 2027.

Overview of the CIHR Health System Impact Fellowship

The Health System Impact Fellowship is organized by CIHR’s Institute of Health Services and Policy Research (IHSPR) in partnership with several CIHR institutes, initiatives and organizations working across areas of health research.

The fellowship is designed around the idea of embedded research. Instead of conducting research exclusively within a university environment, successful fellows become embedded within a host health system organization and work on research that is directly relevant to that organization’s priorities and challenges.

The program is intended to help researchers:

  • Gain practical experience within health system organizations.
  • Apply research and analytical skills to real-world health system challenges.
  • Develop professional and leadership competencies.
  • Build networks across academic and health system environments.
  • Contribute to evidence-informed decision-making.
  • Develop experience working with health system leaders and organizations.
  • Strengthen the capacity of health organizations to use research for learning and improvement.

The fellowship therefore combines academic research with practical experience, professional development, mentorship and networking.

What Does the Health System Impact Fellowship Offer?

The HSI Fellowship has two principal streams.

  1. HSI Award for Doctoral Trainees

The doctoral stream provides a paid one-year experiential learning opportunity.

Doctoral fellows are embedded within their host health system organization and must spend at least 60% of their time working on an impact-oriented embedded research project that is directly relevant to the host organization.

The remaining time, where applicable, is protected for doctoral program commitments such as:

  • Coursework
  • Comprehensive examinations
  • Dissertation work
  • Other approved doctoral responsibilities

The maximum value of the doctoral award is $50,000 for one year.

This includes:

  • $45,000 stipend
  • $5,000 professional development training and research allowance

The structure allows doctoral researchers to continue their academic development while gaining direct experience applying their research capabilities within a health system organization.

  1. HSI Award for Post-Doctoral Researchers

The post-doctoral stream provides a paid two-year experiential learning opportunity.

Post-doctoral researchers must spend at least 70% of their time working with their host health system organization on an impact-oriented embedded research program.

Up to 30% of the fellow’s time may be protected for academic research and related activities under the supervision of their academic supervisor.

The maximum value of the post-doctoral award is $155,000 over two years.

The funding consists of:

  • $70,000 stipend per year
  • $7,500 professional development training and research allowance per year

Certain Northern and international awardees may receive an additional $5,000 per year for professional development training in recognition of higher living and travel costs, subject to the conditions of the opportunity.

Mentorship and Professional Development

The fellowship goes beyond financial support.

Both doctoral and post-doctoral fellows receive a dual supervision and mentorship structure involving:

  1. A health system leader within the host organization; and
  2. An academic supervisor at the fellow’s affiliated university.

This arrangement allows fellows to receive guidance from both the practical health system environment and the academic research environment.

Fellows also participate in professional development and networking through the Health System Impact Training Platform and the annual National Cohort Retreat.

The program specifically emphasizes enriched core competencies, including areas such as leadership and project management.

Research Areas Supported by the Fellowship

The HSI Fellowship covers a broad range of health services, systems and policy research areas.

All applications must first align with the General Pool, which focuses on health services, systems and policy research.

Applicants may also apply to up to two additional funding pools where their research meets the relevant requirements.

The available research areas include:

Health Services, Systems and Policy

The general pool supports research with a primary and substantive focus on health services, health systems and health policy.

Research should align with CIHR’s Pillar 3 research definition, IHSPR’s mandate and one or more of its strategic research priorities.

The proposed research must also address a significant health system challenge or priority identified by the applicant’s host organization.

Primary Health Care

This stream supports research focused on innovations that can transform primary health care delivery systems.

Projects should contribute to the transformation of primary health care and address the Quintuple Aim, which encompasses population health outcomes, patient and care experience, provider satisfaction, value and health equity.

Northern Research

Applicants working with health system organizations located in Yukon, Northwest Territories or Nunavut may qualify for the Northern research area, provided the proposed research aligns with a health system priority in Northern Canada.

Eastern Canada

The Eastern research area covers Newfoundland and Labrador, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick.

Applicants must be embedded within an eligible health system organization in Eastern Canada and their research must address a relevant regional health system priority.

Indigenous Peoples’ Health

This area supports research focused on Indigenous health and wellness.

Applicants must meet the opportunity’s requirements concerning Indigenous identity and/or meaningful, culturally safe and reciprocal engagement with Indigenous Peoples, communities, organizations or governments.

Potential areas include:

  • Indigenous self-determination in health system design.
  • Indigenous-led primary health care models.
  • Health equity and culturally grounded health services.
  • Digital health equity and data governance.
  • Cross-jurisdictional health care coordination.
  • Health system preparedness and resilience.

Aging

Research in this area must align with the CIHR Institute of Aging Strategic Plan 2023–2028.

Cancer

Research must align with the mandate and priorities of the CIHR Institute of Cancer Research, including areas such as:

  • Cancer prevention
  • Early detection
  • Cancer survivorship

Circulatory and Respiratory Health

Projects should align with the relevant CIHR mandate and address at least one stage of the care continuum:

  • Pre-acute care
  • Acute care
  • Post-acute care

Sex, Gender and Health

Research can focus on women’s health and/or Two-Spirit and LGBTQI+ health, subject to the requirements of the relevant research area.

Musculoskeletal Health and Arthritis

Applications must have a primary focus aligned with the mandate of CIHR’s Institute of Musculoskeletal Health and Arthritis.

Nutrition, Metabolism and Diabetes

Research must align with the mandate of CIHR’s Institute of Nutrition, Metabolism and Diabetes.

Infection and Immunity

Projects must align with the mandate of the CIHR Institute of Infection and Immunity.

Pandemic Preparedness and Health Emergencies

This area supports research focused on preparing for or responding to pandemics and other health emergencies.

Population and Public Health

The Population and Public Health stream focuses on core public health functions such as:

  • Disease prevention
  • Health promotion
  • Population health
  • Health equity

The trainee must be hosted by a governmental public health institution or a community-based organization with a public-health-related mandate.

Post-Market Drug Safety and Effectiveness

Research may examine areas including:

  • Drug safety
  • Drug effectiveness
  • Real-World Evidence
  • Pharmacoepidemiology
  • Drug policy
  • Health policy and biostatistics
  • Administrative health data

Patient-Oriented Research

This stream requires alignment with CIHR’s Strategy for Patient-Oriented Research.

Applications must demonstrate co-leadership with people with lived and living experience and community partners, with the research grounded in priorities identified by those partners.

How Much Funding Is Available?

The 2027 competition has substantial funding available across the two fellowship streams.

The source indicates a total amount of approximately $3.2 million for the opportunity, with additional funding associated with Health Research BC. The competition is expected to support approximately 38 awards, although funding is subject to the availability of contributions from CIHR and its partners.

Doctoral Fellowship Funding

Doctoral trainees can receive up to:

$50,000 for one year

Breakdown:

  • $45,000 stipend
  • $5,000 professional development training and research allowance

Post-Doctoral Fellowship Funding

Post-doctoral researchers can receive up to:

$155,000 for two years

Breakdown:

  • $70,000 stipend per year
  • $7,500 professional development training and research allowance per year

The professional development allowance can support eligible expenses associated with professional competency development and participation in program activities, including travel and accommodation related to the National Cohort Retreat.

Partner Matching Contribution Requirement

One important feature of this fellowship is the requirement for a contribution from the host health system organization.

CIHR and Health Research BC can contribute up to 70% of the total award value.

The host health system organization must provide the remaining 30% in cash at the time of application.

For example:

  • For a $50,000 doctoral award, the maximum CIHR/Health Research BC contribution is $35,000, while the remaining $15,000 must come from the host organization.
  • For a $155,000 post-doctoral award, the maximum CIHR/Health Research BC contribution is $108,500, while the remaining $46,500 must be secured from the host organization.

The host organization can obtain the required contribution from alternative sources in certain circumstances, but the required 30% contribution must be confirmed when the application is submitted. Existing CIHR or Tri-Agency grant funds cannot be used for this contribution.

Who Can Apply for the CIHR Health System Impact Fellowship?

The fellowship is specifically designed for doctoral trainees and post-doctoral researchers working in health services and policy research or related fields.

CLICK HERE TO APPLY

Doctoral Stream

For Stream A, the nominated principal applicant must be a trainee who:

  • Is enrolled full-time in a doctoral degree by the award funding start date.
  • Is studying HSPR or a related field.
  • Is undertaking doctoral training at a Canadian CIHR-eligible institution.
  • Has not previously held an HSI doctoral award.

Post-Doctoral Stream

For Stream B, the applicant must:

  • Have obtained a PhD or DrPH in HSPR or a related field, or obtain the degree by the award funding start date.
  • Have not previously held an HSI post-doctoral award.
  • Maintain trainee status throughout the award period.

Examples of related fields include:

  • Health services and systems research
  • Health economics
  • Health policy
  • Population health
  • Indigenous Peoples’ health
  • Artificial intelligence
  • Public health
  • Epidemiology
  • Gerontology
  • Data science

The source states that these are examples and that related fields may extend beyond this list.

Additional Eligibility Requirements

Meeting the academic requirements alone is not sufficient.

Applicants must also satisfy several other conditions.

Click HERE for more information

Applicants Cannot Hold an Independent Research Position

The nominated principal applicant cannot hold or be on leave from an independent research position.

Previous Employment With the Host Organization

The applicant generally cannot be a current or past employee of the proposed host health system organization, nor a current owner or shareholder of the proposed host organization, subject to the special-case exception identified by the program.

Two Supervisors Are Required

Each application must identify both:

Health System Supervisor: A health system leader at the proposed host organization who has committed to hosting and supervising the applicant.

Academic Supervisor: A university-based academic supervisor with an appointment in a Canadian university graduate training program.

For doctoral applicants, the academic supervisor must be the applicant’s primary PhD supervisor.

For post-doctoral applicants, the academic supervisor must secure the applicant’s post-doctoral status at the university by the award start date.

Citizenship and Residency Requirements

The opportunity allows different citizenship categories depending on where the award is held.

For awards held at host health system organizations in Canada, the applicant may be:

  • A Canadian citizen
  • A Canadian permanent resident
  • A Protected Person under subsection 95(2) of Canada’s Immigration and Refugee Protection Act
  • A citizen of another country

For awards held at host health system organizations outside Canada, the applicant must be a:

  • Canadian citizen
  • Canadian permanent resident
  • Protected Person under subsection 95(2) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act

In all cases, the applicant must be registered at an eligible institution at the start of the award.

This means the opportunity is not presented as being restricted to one race or ethnic group. However, applicants must meet the specific institutional, academic, host-organization and citizenship requirements applicable to the proposed fellowship arrangement.

International Applicants and International Research Opportunities

The fellowship does provide for certain international circumstances.

For awards involving a host health system organization located outside Canada, additional citizenship restrictions apply. The eligible international host organization must also meet specific requirements.

An international health system host organization must:

  • Be multinational in scope.
  • Include Canada as a country in its multinational partnership or membership.
  • Offer an HSPR-relevant project to prospective applicants.
  • Ensure the proposed project is applicable to the Canadian context.
  • Have potential to generate learning that can benefit Canada.

Therefore, being located outside Canada does not automatically make an organization eligible to host an HSI Fellow. The organization and proposed research must satisfy the program’s requirements.

What Organizations Can Host a Fellow?

The fellowship permits a broad range of health system organizations to serve as hosts.

Eligible types of organizations may include:

  • National health organizations
  • Ministries of health
  • Community hospitals
  • Academic teaching hospitals
  • Health authorities
  • Public health organizations
  • Health charities
  • Consulting firms undertaking health-related work
  • Pharmaceutical companies
  • Health-related professional associations
  • Indigenous health organizations
  • Public organizations
  • Not-for-profit organizations
  • Private for-profit organizations

The organization may operate at local, regional, provincial/territorial or federal/national levels.

However, universities and research institutes whose primary mandate is to conduct or fund research are not eligible to serve as the host health system organization under this competition.

Partner Linkage Tool

CIHR is providing a Partner Linkage Tool to help applicants connect with organizations interested in hosting doctoral or post-doctoral researchers.

The tool is optional.

Applicants are not required to use the linkage tool or contact organizations listed through it.

CIHR also states that using the tool does not provide an advantage in the evaluation or funding decision.

The information supplied by participating organizations is provided voluntarily and the database is expected to be updated regularly until the application deadline.

Important Research and Indigenous Engagement Requirements

Applications involving Indigenous health or First Nations, Métis and/or Inuit populations are subject to additional requirements.

Where Indigenous populations are involved at any stage of the research, including data collection or data access, the applicant and both supervisors must meet the program’s requirements concerning Indigenous self-identification and/or meaningful and culturally safe involvement with Indigenous Peoples.

The requirements are intended to support:

  • Indigenous leadership in research agendas.
  • Culturally safe research.
  • Respectful relationships with Indigenous communities.
  • Indigenous research methodologies and frameworks.
  • Development of Indigenous trainees and researchers.
  • Indigenous data sovereignty.

Applicants who are required to submit the Indigenous Health Research Cultural Safety Form must do so, as failure to attach the form when required may result in withdrawal of the application.

Equity, Diversity and Inclusion

The fellowship incorporates equity, diversity and inclusion considerations into its research and training environment.

CIHR states that the program seeks to support the inclusion and advancement of groups that have historically experienced exclusion from science and research.

The program objectives specifically recognize emerging researchers from equity-denied communities and groups that have historically faced systemic barriers within the research ecosystem, including:

  • Indigenous Peoples
  • Communities affected by racism
  • Persons with disabilities
  • Members of 2SLGBTQI+ communities
  • Groups experiencing gender-based barriers

Applicants are expected to integrate equity, diversity and inclusion considerations, including sex and gender considerations, and Indigenous Rights considerations where appropriate to their research design and practices.

Time Commitment During the Fellowship

The fellowship requires significant engagement with the host organization.

Doctoral Fellows

Doctoral awardees must spend between 60% and 100% of their time working with the host health system organization on an embedded research project or program.

Any remaining time may be devoted to doctoral commitments.

The program explains that 60% corresponds approximately to three days per week based on a 37.5-hour work week, although the time does not have to be distributed equally every week.

Post-Doctoral Fellows

Post-doctoral awardees must spend between 70% and 100% of their time working with the host health system organization.

Any remaining time may be dedicated to academic research and related activities, including publishing, teaching or developing a research program under the academic supervisor.

Both streams also require participation in professional development activities and the Health System Impact Training Platform.

Professional Development Requirements

Successful fellows are expected to actively participate in professional development.

Each awardee must identify at least three enriched core competencies for development during the fellowship.

The professional development and research allowance can support expenses associated with eligible training and competency development.

Awardees must also participate in:

  • Orientation activities.
  • The annual HSI Conference/National Cohort Retreat.
  • Professional development training.
  • Health System Impact Training Platform activities.

These activities are intended to complement the research experience with leadership, professional and networking opportunities.

Can Applicants Apply for Other Awards?

Applicants may apply for the HSI Fellowship and other federal awards programs during the same year.

However, applicants cannot receive funding from more than one federal award at the same time.

Where another federal award is held, the funding may need to be formally deferred or interrupted before HSI Fellowship funding begins.

The program also specifies that all awards must begin on September 1, 2027, and deferment is not permitted.

Application Deadline and Important Dates

Applicants should pay close attention to the competition timeline.

Key Dates

  • Program launch: September 24, 2026
  • Application deadline: January 12, 2027
  • Anticipated notice of decision: August 11, 2027
  • Funding start date: September 1, 2027

The application deadline is therefore January 12, 2027. Applicants should allow sufficient time to identify a host organization, secure supervisors, develop the research proposal and complete the required application components.

What Applicants Need to Prepare

Applicants should familiarize themselves with the official HSI Fellowship application instructions before beginning their application.

The application requirements include several important administrative components.

Applicants and supervisors must have:

  • A ResearchNet account.
  • A CIHR PIN.
  • A completed Self-identification Questionnaire.
  • An updated My CIHR Profile.
  • The appropriate institutional affiliation information.

A new requirement for this competition is that the nominated principal applicant must submit a Tri-Agency CV (TCV).

Supervisors do not need to submit a TCV. Instead, the applicant is responsible for providing a narrative description of the research team’s expertise and experience.

Applicants are also required to complete one of CIHR’s three interactive modules on sex and gender in research and include the certificate of completion with the application.

How Applications Are Evaluated

Applications go through a relevance review and peer-review process.

All applications must be relevant to the mandate of the Institute of Health Services and Policy Research (IHSPR) and the General Pool.

Applications submitted to additional research pools are also reviewed for relevance to those particular areas.

An application that does not meet the requirements of a particular additional pool may remain active if it remains relevant to another eligible pool, including the General Pool.

Peer review is conducted according to CIHR’s peer-review principles, with the process also referencing the San Francisco Declaration on Research Assessment (DORA).

The funding decision process provides that funding is distributed to applications in the relevant pools and subsequently across the competition according to the program’s stated funding process.

The source states that applications receiving a rating below 3.5 will not be funded.

What Happens After an Award Is Offered?

Successful applicants must accept the award within 15 working days of the date of the offer.

If an award is not accepted within that period, the award may be cancelled and offered to the next fundable applicant.

The fellowship must begin on September 1, 2027.

Doctoral applicants must provide official confirmation of registration in their doctoral program before starting the award.

Post-doctoral applicants must provide official confirmation that their PhD requirements have been completed, including the required evidence concerning graduation, oral defense or a confirmed oral defense date.

Reporting and Participation Requirements

Fellows are required to participate in monitoring and evaluation activities associated with the program.

The nominated principal applicant must complete:

  • Enriched Core Competency Self-Assessments.
  • A final report containing an Impact Narrative.

The fellow may also be required to participate in evaluation studies, surveys, workshops and audits and provide relevant data or reports to assist CIHR in assessing the progress and results of its programs.

For research involving First Nations, Inuit or Métis communities whose traditional and ancestral territories are in Canada, data must be managed according to the data-management principles established and approved by the relevant communities, including considerations relating to Indigenous data sovereignty and free, prior and informed consent.

Why the Health System Impact Fellowship Is Different

The HSI Fellowship is structured around the connection between research and practical health system impact.

Rather than limiting fellows’ activities to academic research, the program places them inside health system organizations where they can observe how decisions are made and how evidence can contribute to organizational learning and improvement.

The fellowship therefore combines several components:

  1. Financial support through stipends and professional development allowances.
  2. Embedded research experience within a health system organization.
  3. Academic supervision through a university-based supervisor.
  4. Health system mentorship from an organizational leader.
  5. Professional competency development.
  6. Networking opportunities.
  7. Exposure to evidence-informed decision-making.
  8. Opportunities to contribute to health system improvement.

This structure is intended to develop researchers who can work across academic and health system environments.

Important Considerations Before Applying

Potential applicants should carefully examine the eligibility requirements before investing significant time in an application.

In particular, applicants should establish:

  • Whether their doctoral or post-doctoral field qualifies as HSPR or a related field.
  • Whether they will have the required doctoral status by September 1, 2027.
  • Whether they can identify an eligible host health system organization.
  • Whether an appropriate health system supervisor is available.
  • Whether an eligible Canadian academic supervisor is available.
  • Whether the host organization can secure the required 30% financial contribution.
  • Whether their proposed research fits the General Pool.
  • Whether they qualify for an additional research area.
  • Whether they meet the relevant citizenship and residency requirements.
  • Whether they can satisfy the required sex and gender research training.
  • Whether they can commit the required proportion of time to the host organization.
  • Whether they can meet the September 1, 2027 start date.

These requirements are particularly important because the fellowship is not simply a conventional scholarship or academic stipend. It requires a structured relationship among the researcher, academic institution and host health system organization.

Conclusion

The CIHR Health System Impact Fellowship 2027 provides a structured opportunity for doctoral trainees and post-doctoral researchers in health services and policy research and related disciplines to combine academic research with practical experience inside health system organizations.

The program offers up to $50,000 for one year for doctoral trainees and up to $155,000 for two years for post-doctoral researchers, together with professional development, mentorship, networking and embedded research experience.

The fellowship covers a wide range of research areas, including health policy, health systems, primary health care, public health, population health, Indigenous health, aging, cancer, sex and gender, pandemic preparedness, patient-oriented research, drug safety and effectiveness, and other related areas.

However, applicants must satisfy detailed eligibility conditions involving academic status, research field, host organizations, supervisors, citizenship or residency, funding contributions and research alignment.

For researchers who meet these requirements, the program provides an opportunity to develop experience at the intersection of research, health policy, health systems and evidence-informed decision-making.

The application deadline is January 12, 2027, with the anticipated notice of decision scheduled for August 11, 2027, and the funding start date set for September 1, 2027.

Discover more global fellowship opportunities on Opportunities for Youth (OFY) HERE

Prospective applicants should review the complete HSI Fellowship application instructions and eligibility requirements carefully before submitting an application.

The European Commission Joint Research Centre (JRC) is currently advertising a wide range of Auxiliary Contract Staff vacancies across several of its scientific, technical, policy and administrative locations in Europe.

The current recruitment round includes opportunities for professionals working in areas such as clean energy innovation, wind energy, quantitative policy analysis, artificial intelligence, crop monitoring, transport, cybersecurity, sustainable industry, nuclear science, economics, climate action, bioenergy, human resources and knowledge management.

These vacancies are distributed across several JRC locations, including Ispra, Petten, Seville, Karlsruhe and Geel, providing opportunities to work within different scientific and policy environments of the European Commission.

The positions listed on the JRC Recruitment Portal are primarily classified at FGIII or FGIV grade and are offered as Auxiliary Contract Staff positions.

Importantly, these are not a single job opening or one general recruitment programme. Each vacancy represents a separate position with its own job description, location, deadline and potentially different professional and educational requirements.

Applicants should therefore identify the position that best matches their qualifications and carefully review the individual vacancy notice before submitting an application.

Overview of the European Commission JRC Vacancies

The current vacancies cover a broad range of professional fields, including:

  • Clean energy innovation
  • Wind energy sustainability
  • Quantitative policy analysis
  • Survey design and analysis
  • Indicator frameworks
  • Impact evaluation
  • Artificial intelligence
  • Crop monitoring and modelling
  • Transport and AI applications
  • AI cybersecurity
  • Sustainable industry
  • Energy security
  • Nuclear science
  • Knowledge management
  • Events organization
  • Nuclear safeguards

  • Urban climate action
  • Bioenergy

  • Human resources
  • Learning, talent and career development

What Is the Joint Research Centre?

The Joint Research Centre (JRC) is the European Commission’s scientific service and operates through research and technical activities connected with European policy priorities.

The recruitment portal lists positions across multiple JRC sites and scientific areas.

The vacancies in this recruitment round demonstrate the breadth of expertise required within the JRC, ranging from highly specialized scientific and technical research to policy analysis, administration and organizational support.

Understanding how people think, make decisions, and respond to policies is increasingly important for governments, development organizations, researchers, and policy professionals. Policies can be technically sound and still produce limited results if they do not take into account how people actually behave in real-world situations.

To help professionals and researchers develop a stronger understanding of this field, the World Bank Group Institute for Economic Development offers the Introduction to Behavioral Science in Public Policy: New Edition, a virtual e-learning course designed to introduce participants to the fundamental principles of behavioral science and their application to public policy and international development.

The course explores how people’s automatic thinking, social environment, mental models, and cognitive biases influence decisions and actions. It also demonstrates how these behavioral factors can affect the effectiveness of government policies and development programs.

The training covers practical applications across areas such as education, healthcare, social norms, gender equality, tax compliance, climate change, and other international development challenges.

For students, researchers, development professionals, policymakers, and other individuals interested in public policy, this course provides an opportunity to understand how behavioral science can be incorporated into the design of more effective policies and programs.

About the World Bank Behavioral Science Course

The course is presented by the World Bank Group Institute for Economic Development and introduces participants to the World Bank’s approach to behavioral science.

According to the course information, the World Bank has developed its behavioral science methodologies through collaboration with approximately 70 partners while supporting governments across more than 100 countries.

The training is particularly relevant because traditional policy design often assumes that people will respond to incentives and information in predictable ways. Behavioral science adds another dimension by examining how people actually make decisions, including the influence of habits, social expectations, cognitive shortcuts, beliefs, and the way information is presented.

The course therefore provides participants with an introduction to how behavioral insights can be incorporated into public policy and development programs.

What Is Behavioral Science in Public Policy?

Behavioral science examines the factors that influence human behavior and decision-making.

In public policy, behavioral science can help policymakers and development practitioners understand why people may respond differently to policies than traditional economic or rational-choice models might predict.

For example, people may:

  • Make decisions automatically rather than carefully analyzing every option.
  • Be influenced by the behavior and expectations of people around them.
  • Interpret information according to existing beliefs or mental models.
  • Respond differently depending on how choices are presented.
  • Be influenced by cognitive biases.
  • Make decisions under pressure or with limited information.

Understanding these behaviors can help policymakers design programs that better reflect how people actually behave.

The World Bank course introduces these concepts and demonstrates how they can be applied to real development and policy challenges.

Why Behavioral Science Matters for Public Policy

Behavioral science has applications across a wide range of policy areas.

The course highlights applications in areas including:

Education

Behavioral insights can help policymakers understand factors that influence students’ learning, attendance, motivation, and educational decisions.

Healthcare

Behavioral science can contribute to understanding decisions related to healthcare access, treatment adherence, preventive care, and health-related behavior.

Social Norms

People’s behavior is often influenced by what they believe others expect or what they perceive as normal within their communities.

Understanding social norms can therefore help development practitioners design more effective interventions.

Gender Equality

Behavioral and social factors can influence opportunities, expectations, decisions, and participation related to gender.

Behavioral insights can help policymakers better understand these factors when designing programs aimed at improving gender equality.

Tax Compliance

The course includes a case study on tax compliance in Kosovo, demonstrating how behavioral science can be applied to government policy and taxpayer behavior.

Climate Change

Behavioral science can also contribute to understanding how individuals and communities respond to environmental information, incentives, social expectations, and climate-related policies.

These examples demonstrate that behavioral science is not limited to one particular sector. Its principles can potentially be applied across many areas of public policy and international development.

Key Learning Objectives

The course is designed to give participants an introductory understanding of behavioral science and its relevance to international development.

By completing the training, participants are expected to develop knowledge in several important areas.

1. Understand Behavioral Science Principles

Participants will gain an introductory understanding of behavioral science principles and how they can be applied to public policy.

The course connects behavioral concepts with international development and the design of policies and programs intended to produce stronger outcomes.

2. Understand Automatic Thinking

One major component of the course focuses on how people think automatically.

Participants explore the ways people make decisions without consciously processing every piece of available information.

The course uses videos, readings, a brain game, and a case study to explore this area.

3. Understand Social Thinking

The training also examines how people think socially.

Human behavior does not occur in isolation. Social environments, expectations, norms, and interactions with other people can significantly influence decisions.

The course uses a case study involving social norms in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region to illustrate these concepts.

4. Understand Mental Models

Another major focus is the role of mental models in decision-making.

Mental models influence how people understand situations, interpret information, and approach problems.

The course includes a case study involving Peru and growth mindset to demonstrate the relevance of these concepts.

5. Apply Behavioral Insights to Policy Design

Beyond learning theoretical concepts, participants are introduced to how behavioral insights can be used in designing public policies and development programs.

This makes the training particularly relevant to people working in government, international development, research, economics, social policy, and related fields.

Course Duration and Format

The training is designed as a relatively short online learning experience.

According to the provided course information:

  • Duration: 6 hours
  • Number of videos: 8
  • Training format: E-learning
  • Community: Multiple discussion forums
  • Assessments: Included
  • Certification: Included

Because the course is delivered online, participants can access the learning materials without needing to attend a traditional physical classroom.

This format can make the course suitable for professionals, students, and researchers who want to develop additional knowledge while continuing their existing studies or work.

What Is Included in the Course?

The World Bank behavioral science course includes several different types of learning materials and activities.

Participants can expect access to:

  • Video lessons
  • Text-based learning materials
  • Assessments
  • Interactive games
  • Case studies
  • Discussion forums
  • Mandatory and recommended readings
  • Knowledge-check examinations
  • A final assessment
  • A certificate upon completion

The combination of videos, readings, assessments, games, and discussions provides participants with different ways to engage with the subject.

Detailed Course Curriculum

The course is divided into five major sections.

Module 1: Welcome and Introduction

The first section introduces participants to the course and establishes the foundation for the remaining lessons.

It includes:

  • Welcome and introduction
  • Frequently Asked Questions
  • Participant introductions
  • Mandatory pre-course assessment
  • Expectations and learner review
  • Course completion requirements
  • Course syllabus
  • Introduction video
  • Mandatory reading
  • Discussion forum

The introductory section helps participants understand how the course is organized and what is expected of them.

The pre-course assessment is mandatory, making it an important part of the enrollment and learning process.

Module 2: We Think Automatically

The second section focuses on automatic thinking and how it affects human decisions.

The module includes:

  • Keynote address on automatic thinking
  • Video lesson
  • Key concepts
  • Interactive brain game
  • Tax compliance case study in Kosovo
  • Kosovo case study video
  • Mandatory reading
  • Glossary
  • Discussion forum
  • Recommended readings
  • Knowledge Check Exam #1

The Tax Compliance in Kosovo case study provides participants with a practical example of how behavioral science can be connected to government policy.

The interactive brain game also provides a practical way for learners to explore some of the concepts introduced in the module.

Module 3: We Think Socially

The third section explores the social dimensions of human behavior.

The module includes:

  • Keynote address on social thinking
  • Video lesson
  • Case study concerning social norms in MENA
  • MENA case study video
  • Mandatory reading
  • Glossary
  • Discussion forum
  • Recommended readings
  • Knowledge Check Exam #2

Social norms are particularly important in development because people’s decisions can be strongly influenced by what they believe other people do, expect, approve of, or consider acceptable.

Understanding these influences can help policymakers develop interventions that account for the social environment in which policies operate.

Module 4: We Think With Mental Models

The fourth section focuses on mental models and their role in human decision-making.

It includes:

  • Keynote address on mental models
  • Interactive brain game
  • Wavy Lines activity
  • Video lesson on mental models
  • Peru and Growth Mindset case study
  • Peru case study video
  • Mandatory reading
  • Recommended readings
  • Glossary
  • Discussion forum
  • Knowledge Check Exam #3

The module introduces learners to the idea that individuals interpret the world through mental frameworks that can affect how they understand information and make decisions.

The Peru and Growth Mindset case study provides an applied example of these concepts.

Module 5: Conclusion

The final section brings together the concepts covered throughout the training.

It includes:

  • Final thoughts
  • Course conclusion
  • Reflection discussion forum
  • Mandatory post-course final assessment
  • Participant feedback
  • Acknowledgments
  • Certificate

The post-course assessment is mandatory.

Participants who complete the required components can receive a certificate, providing formal recognition of their completion of the training.

Who Is This World Bank Course Designed For?

The course information specifically identifies policy practitioners and researchers who are interested in applying behavioral science to public policy on development topics as the intended audience.

This makes the course potentially relevant to people working or studying in fields such as:

  • Public policy
  • International development
  • Economics
  • Political science
  • Development studies
  • Public administration
  • Government
  • Social policy
  • Research
  • International organizations
  • Non-governmental organizations
  • Behavioral science
  • Social sciences

It can also be useful for students and early-career professionals who want to learn more about the relationship between human behavior and policy design.

Is This Course Useful for International Development Careers?

Behavioral science is increasingly relevant to international development because development programs ultimately depend on human behavior.

A government may introduce a policy, an organization may develop a program, or an institution may provide information, but the actual results can depend on how individuals and communities respond.

Learning about behavioral science can therefore provide another perspective for people interested in development-related careers.

The course may be particularly useful for individuals interested in working with:

  • Government institutions
  • International development organizations
  • Research institutions
  • Non-governmental organizations
  • International financial institutions
  • Public policy organizations
  • Social development programs
  • Economic development initiatives

For students and professionals interested in international development, the course can also complement knowledge in economics, public administration, political science, development studies, data analysis, and related disciplines.

Practical Topics Covered by the Course

One of the strengths of the training is its focus on practical examples rather than presenting behavioral science only as an abstract academic subject.

The course connects behavioral concepts to real-world development and policy challenges.

Some of the highlighted applications include:

Tax compliance: Understanding behavioral factors that influence whether individuals comply with taxation requirements.

Social norms: Examining how people’s behavior is affected by the expectations and behavior of others.

Growth mindset: Exploring behavioral concepts through a case study from Peru.

Healthcare: Considering how behavioral science can contribute to health-related policies.

Education: Applying behavioral insights to education-related challenges.

Gender equality: Examining behavioral and social factors relevant to gender-related policy.

Climate change: Understanding behavioral dimensions of environmental policy and climate action.

These examples demonstrate the broad potential application of behavioral science across public policy.

Interactive Learning and Assessments

The course is not limited to watching videos.

Participants are expected to engage with multiple learning activities, including:

  • Brain games
  • Case studies
  • Discussion forums
  • Mandatory readings
  • Recommended readings
  • Knowledge-check examinations
  • Pre-course assessment
  • Final assessment

This structure allows learners to engage with the concepts in several different ways.

The discussion forums also provide an opportunity for participants to reflect on the material and interact around the course topics.

Certificate of Completion

A certificate is included among the course components.

The certificate is presented at the conclusion of the course after participants complete the required components.

For students and professionals, a certificate can serve as evidence of participation and completion of an additional professional learning activity.

However, participants should distinguish between a short online course certificate and an academic degree or professional license. The course is designed as an e-learning training program rather than a university degree program.

Course Trainers and World Bank Behavioral Science Team

The course information identifies several members of the World Bank’s behavioral science team.

Renos Vakis

Renos Vakis is identified as the Head of the Mind, Behavior, and Development Unit (eMBeD).

Dana Qarout

Dana Qarout is identified as a Behavioral Scientist with the Mind, Behavior & Development Unit (eMBeD).

Jonathan Karver

Jonathan Karver is identified as an Economist with the Mind, Behavior and Development Unit (eMBeD) within Development Impact (DIME).

The involvement of professionals from the World Bank’s behavioral science and development teams provides participants with exposure to perspectives connected to international development practice.

Enrollment Information

Enrollment for the course is described as open in the supplied information.

The course page instructs interested participants to enroll and indicates that registered trainees can access the course materials according to the schedule of the relevant edition.

The supplied page states that course content for enrolled trainees would become available from May 12, 2025.

Because this date has passed, prospective learners should verify the current course edition and availability directly through the official World Bank Institute course platform before relying on the historical enrollment information.

Official course page: World Bank Institute — Introduction to Behavioral Science in Public Policy

Important Date and Deadline Information

The supplied course information does not provide a specific final application deadline.

Instead, it states:

  • Enrollment was open.
  • Course content for enrolled trainees was scheduled to become available from May 12, 2025.
  • No separate closing date for applications was provided.

Since the stated course-access date is from a previous edition, applicants should check the official World Bank course platform for the latest enrollment information and any new deadline.

How to Enroll

Interested participants can begin by visiting the World Bank Institute’s online course platform.

The general process involves:

  1. Visit the official World Bank Institute course platform.
  2. Locate the Introduction to Behavioral Science in Public Policy course.
  3. Review the current course information and enrollment status.
  4. Create an account or sign in if required.
  5. Enroll in the course.
  6. Complete the required pre-course assessment.
  7. Work through the video lessons, readings, activities, and case studies.
  8. Participate in the required discussion activities.
  9. Complete the knowledge checks.
  10. Complete the mandatory post-course assessment.
  11. Follow the course requirements for receiving the certificate.

Applicants should always follow the instructions displayed on the current official course page because course schedules and enrollment procedures can change between editions.

Enroll Now

Why Learn Behavioral Science?

Behavioral science provides a useful perspective for understanding the gap between how policies are designed and how people actually respond to them.

Traditional policy approaches may focus heavily on economic incentives, regulations, resources, or information. Behavioral science adds another layer by asking questions such as:

  • How do people actually make decisions?
  • What happens when people are under pressure?
  • How do social expectations influence behavior?
  • Why do people sometimes behave differently from what policymakers expect?
  • How do existing beliefs influence decisions?
  • How can programs be designed around real human behavior?
  • How can behavioral insights improve policy outcomes?

These questions are particularly important in international development, where policies and programs operate across diverse social, economic, and cultural environments.

Benefits of Taking the Course

Participants can potentially gain several benefits from completing the training.

Develop Knowledge of Behavioral Science

The course provides an introduction to important behavioral science concepts and terminology.

Understand Human Decision-Making

Participants explore automatic thinking, social thinking, and mental models and how these processes influence decisions.

Connect Theory With Real-World Policy

Case studies help demonstrate how behavioral science can be applied to actual development and policy challenges.

Strengthen Public Policy Knowledge

The course can complement existing knowledge in public policy, economics, development studies, public administration, and related disciplines.

Learn From World Bank Approaches

Participants are introduced to behavioral science methodologies associated with the World Bank’s work in international development.

Gain an Online Certificate

Participants who meet the course requirements can receive a certificate of completion.

Study Flexibly Online

Because the training is delivered through an e-learning platform, participants can study remotely rather than attending a physical training location.

Final Thoughts

The Introduction to Behavioral Science in Public Policy: New Edition provides an introduction to an increasingly important area of public policy and international development.

Rather than looking only at policies, regulations, incentives, or resources, behavioral science considers the people who ultimately interact with and respond to those policies. The course introduces participants to three major ways of understanding human thinking: automatic thinking, social thinking, and thinking through mental models.

Through videos, readings, interactive games, case studies, discussion forums, assessments, and practical examples, participants can explore how behavioral insights may be applied to areas such as education, healthcare, taxation, gender equality, social norms, and climate change.

The course is particularly relevant to policy practitioners and researchers interested in applying behavioral science to development-related public policy, while people studying or working in international development, economics, public administration, social sciences, and related fields may also find the subject valuable.

The training is approximately 6 hours long, delivered online, and includes a certificate upon successful completion of the required activities.

However, prospective applicants should pay close attention to the course’s current status. The supplied information refers to content becoming available from May 12, 2025, and does not state a final application deadline. Since that date has passed, applicants should visit the official World Bank Institute course platform to determine whether a new edition is currently available and to confirm the latest enrollment dates and requirements.

Stay updated with new World Bank courses, learning opportunities, and future editions by subscribing to the official newsletter.

item.content:encoded:
The Westerwelle Foundation for International Understanding is inviting eligible national service candidates to apply for three National Service positions at the Westerwelle Startup Haus Accra (WSHAC) in Accra, Ghana. The available positions are Operations & Admin Assistant, Programs Assistant, and Community & Marketing Assistant.

These opportunities provide an opportunity for young professionals to gain practical experience within an international entrepreneurship and innovation ecosystem while contributing to the development of one of Ghana’s newest startup hubs.

Application Deadline: Applications are accepted on a rolling basis.

About the Westerwelle Foundation

The Westerwelle Foundation for International Understanding is a non-profit organization headquartered in Berlin, Germany. The Foundation was established in 2013 by Dr. Guido Westerwelle, former German Minister for Foreign Affairs, and Ralph Dommermuth, CEO and Founder of United Internet AG.

The Foundation focuses on accelerating digital transformation in emerging economies and supporting positive developments that contribute to transparency, integrity, innovation, entrepreneurship, and stronger institutions.

One of the Foundation’s key initiatives is the Westerwelle Startup Haus, a network of entrepreneurship hubs designed to support entrepreneurs, innovators, and emerging businesses through access to workspaces, networks, mentoring, entrepreneurship programmes, and other forms of ecosystem support.

The Westerwelle Startup Haus network includes locations in:

  • Tunis, Tunisia
  • Kigali, Rwanda
  • Arusha, Tanzania
  • Mombasa, Kenya
  • Accra, Ghana

Through these hubs, the Foundation seeks to strengthen entrepreneurship ecosystems and facilitate collaboration between founders, investors, corporations, universities, development organizations, and other ecosystem partners.

About Westerwelle Startup Haus Accra

The Westerwelle Startup Haus Accra is based in Accra, Ghana, and is being developed as a collaborative entrepreneurship and innovation hub.

The hub brings together a wide range of stakeholders, including:

  • Startup founders
  • Entrepreneurs
  • Innovators
  • Investors
  • Corporates
  • Universities
  • Mentors
  • Facilitators
  • Ecosystem partners

WSHAC provides flexible workspaces, entrepreneurship programmes, networking opportunities, and strategic partnerships intended to help entrepreneurs build and grow scalable businesses.

The Accra hub also aims to contribute to Ghana’s broader innovation ecosystem by creating opportunities for collaboration and knowledge exchange across Ghana, Africa, and international markets.

For national service candidates, working at WSHAC provides exposure to an environment where entrepreneurship, innovation, communications, programme delivery, administration, community engagement, and business support intersect.

Available Westerwelle Startup Haus Accra National Service Positions

There are currently three National Service opportunities available at Westerwelle Startup Haus Accra.

1. National Service Position: Operations & Admin Assistant

Location: Accra, Ghana

Application Deadline: Rolling basis

The Operations & Admin Assistant will support the day-to-day running of the Westerwelle Startup Haus Accra while also assisting with finance and administrative functions.

The position is particularly suited to candidates who are organized, detail-oriented, reliable, comfortable working with documentation, and interested in administration, finance, logistics, procurement, or office operations.

Key Responsibilities

The successful candidate will support several areas of the Haus’s daily operations.

Facilities and Office Operations

Responsibilities will include:

  • Logging maintenance issues involving electricity, internet connectivity, air conditioning, printers, furniture, and other office facilities.
  • Following up with service providers until maintenance and operational issues are fully resolved.
  • Monitoring stock levels for stationery, printing materials, kitchen supplies, and cleaning products.
  • Raising supply requests before essential items run out.
  • Supporting room setup and resetting rooms following meetings, training sessions, programmes, and events.
  • Maintaining the office inventory.
  • Maintaining the fixed asset register.

The role therefore requires someone who can identify operational problems, follow up consistently, and ensure that outstanding issues are not left unresolved.

Documentation and Filing

The Operations & Admin Assistant will also be responsible for supporting accurate and organized documentation.

Duties include:

  • Collecting and filing supplier invoices.
  • Organizing contracts and delivery notes.
  • Maintaining tax certificates and receipts.
  • Maintaining the digital filing structure in SharePoint.
  • Maintaining supplier records in Airtable.
  • Following established document naming conventions.
  • Scanning and indexing physical documents.
  • Keeping finance-related files organized and audit-ready throughout the year.

Attention to detail and confidentiality are particularly important because the position involves financial and commercial documentation.

Procurement Support

The position also provides exposure to procurement-related activities.

The successful candidate will:

  • Request supplier quotations when instructed.
  • Compile quotations for evaluation.
  • Maintain the supplier database.
  • Keep supplier registration information up to date.
  • Track VAT and tax clearance documentation.
  • Track deliveries against purchase orders.
  • Confirm that ordered goods have been received.

Finance Support

The Operations & Admin Assistant will work under supervision to support basic finance processes.

Responsibilities include:

  • Assisting with transaction entry into the accounting system.
  • Supporting preparation of the monthly document pack for the accountant.
  • Following up on outstanding member and client invoices.

Candidates should therefore be comfortable working with numbers, records, spreadsheets, and confidential information.

General Administration

The role will also involve supporting travel and logistics arrangements, including:

  • Travel bookings
  • Accommodation arrangements
  • Logistics for staff
  • Logistics for facilitators
  • Logistics for guests

Qualifications and Experience

Applicants for the Operations & Admin Assistant position should have:

  • A Bachelor’s degree or HND in accounting, finance, business administration, logistics, or a related discipline.
  • Eligibility for the 2026/2027 national service cycle.
  • Strong Excel skills.
  • Willingness to learn QuickBooks or the accounting system selected by WSHAC.
  • A practical and persistent approach to dealing with service providers.
  • The ability to follow issues through to resolution.
  • Strong discretion when handling confidential financial and commercial information.
  • Demonstrable integrity and reliability.
  • References supporting the applicant’s integrity and reliability.

APPLY HERE

2. National Service Position: Programs Assistant

Location: Accra, Ghana

Application Deadline: Rolling basis

The Programs Assistant will support the delivery of Westerwelle Startup Haus Accra’s programme calendar.

The role includes supporting programme outreach, participant coordination, session logistics, data management, reporting, community follow-up, and engagement with mentors, facilitators, experts, and startup founders.

The position may be particularly relevant to candidates with backgrounds in business, economics, development studies, social sciences, communications, or related disciplines who have an interest in entrepreneurship and Ghana’s startup ecosystem.

Key Responsibilities

Programme Delivery

The Programs Assistant will help ensure that programmes and sessions are delivered efficiently and according to schedule.

Responsibilities include:

  • Supporting outreach activities.
  • Publishing programme calls.
  • Responding to applicant enquiries.
  • Compiling applications for review.
  • Maintaining participant lists.
  • Maintaining participant contact records.
  • Maintaining attendance logs.
  • Preparing session materials.
  • Preparing name badges.
  • Preparing handouts.
  • Preparing feedback forms.
  • Coordinating room setup.
  • Coordinating equipment requirements.
  • Coordinating refreshments with the Operations & Admin Support and front desk teams.
  • Liaising with speakers, trainers, and mentors.
  • Supporting scheduling and briefing processes.
  • Assisting with logistics on programme days.

Data and Reporting

Accurate programme data will be an important part of the position.

The Programs Assistant will:

  • Record attendance information.
  • Record participant feedback.
  • Update participant data.
  • Ensure programme data is entered within the same week as each session.
  • Maintain the programme tracker.
  • Identify and flag delays against the delivery calendar.
  • Draft short session reports.
  • Collect participant and stakeholder quotes.
  • Collect photographs.
  • Gather case study material.
  • Share relevant content with the Community & Marketing Assistant for publication.

This means the role combines programme coordination with administrative, reporting, and communication responsibilities.

Community Engagement and Follow-Up

The Programs Assistant will also support ongoing relationships with the entrepreneurship community.

Responsibilities include:

  • Maintaining the mentor database.
  • Maintaining expert contact information.
  • Maintaining facilitator records.
  • Following up with founders.
  • Tracking actions agreed during programmes.
  • Following up on deadlines.
  • Following up on submissions between programme sessions.

Qualifications and Experience

Applicants should have:

  • A degree in business, economics, development studies, social sciences, communications, or a related field.
  • Eligibility for the 2026/2027 national service cycle.
  • Strong written English.
  • The ability to write clear emails.
  • The ability to prepare concise reports without extensive editing.
  • Strong organizational skills.
  • The ability to work toward deadlines.
  • The ability to manage details across several activities at the same time.
  • Confidence when interacting with founders, facilitators, and senior guests.
  • Strong Excel or Google Sheets skills.
  • Willingness to learn Airtable.
  • A genuine interest in entrepreneurship and Ghana’s startup ecosystem.

APPLY HERE

3. National Service Position: Community & Marketing Assistant

Location: Accra, Ghana

Application Deadline: Rolling basis

The Community & Marketing Assistant combines front-of-house, community engagement, content creation, social media, digital communications, and event support responsibilities.

The position is particularly relevant for candidates interested in communications, marketing, journalism, digital content, social media management, photography, videography, hospitality, and community engagement.

The successful candidate will serve as an important point of contact for members, visitors, prospective clients, founders, and other stakeholders visiting the Westerwelle Startup Haus Accra.

The role will also involve transforming activities at the Haus into content for social media, newsletters, websites, and other communication channels.

Key Responsibilities

Front-of-House and Member Support

The Community & Marketing Assistant will help maintain a professional and welcoming environment at the Haus.

Responsibilities include:

  • Opening and closing reception.
  • Ensuring the reception area remains presentable.
  • Maintaining the appearance of the lobby and common areas.
  • Welcoming visitors.
  • Registering visitors.
  • Issuing visitor passes.
  • Directing guests to their hosts.
  • Answering the main telephone line.
  • Monitoring the general enquiries inbox.
  • Responding to enquiries where appropriate.
  • Escalating enquiries when necessary.
  • Checking in members and day-pass users.
  • Maintaining accurate daily occupancy records.
  • Managing meeting room bookings.
  • Managing boardroom bookings.
  • Managing call booth bookings.
  • Resolving scheduling conflicts.
  • Providing campus tours to prospective members.
  • Handing serious membership or business enquiries to the appropriate colleague on the same day.
  • Maintaining the member directory.
  • Maintaining access records in Airtable.

Content Creation and Social Media

A major component of this position is content creation and digital communications.

The successful candidate will:

  • Photograph Haus events.
  • Film programme sessions.
  • Capture community activities and moments.
  • Edit short-form videos.
  • Edit photographs and other visual assets.
  • Draft social media captions.
  • Prepare event recaps.
  • Write short articles.
  • Follow the communication tone of WSHAC.
  • Schedule social media content.
  • Publish content across WSHAC’s social media channels.
  • Follow the established content calendar.
  • Support monthly newsletters.
  • Draft newsletter content.
  • Select suitable images.
  • Maintain newsletter distribution lists.
  • Keep website events pages updated.
  • Keep website news pages updated.
  • Keep team pages current.
  • Maintain an organized media library.
  • Apply appropriate file naming and folder structures.

This makes the opportunity particularly relevant to candidates with practical experience in social media management, photography, videography, graphic design, content creation, digital marketing, or communications.

Brand and Community Engagement

The Community & Marketing Assistant will also contribute to brand consistency and community storytelling.

Responsibilities include:

  • Applying Westerwelle Foundation brand guidelines to content and communication materials.
  • Monitoring social media engagement.
  • Preparing simple monthly performance figures.
  • Collecting founder stories.
  • Collecting member stories.
  • Developing stories that can support reporting.
  • Identifying content that can be used for marketing.
  • Collecting stories that may contribute to fundraising communications.

Event Support

The position also involves supporting events held at the Haus.

Responsibilities include:

  • Supporting registration.
  • Managing guest check-in.
  • Assisting with event signage.
  • Supporting wayfinding.
  • Helping with guest handling during events.
  • Supporting other event-day requirements.

Qualifications and Experience

Applicants for the Community & Marketing Assistant position should have:

  • A Bachelor’s degree or HND in communications, marketing, journalism, hospitality, business administration, or a related discipline.
  • Eligibility for the 2026/2027 national service cycle.
  • Strong interpersonal skills.
  • A warm, confident, and professional approach to visitors and community members.
  • Strong organizational skills.
  • Reliability and attention to detail.
  • The ability to maintain accurate records.
  • Competence with a camera, including the use of a good smartphone camera.
  • Experience with at least one editing tool such as Canva, CapCut, or Adobe Creative Suite.
  • Clear spoken and written English.
  • A strong understanding of tone and communication.
  • Twi or another Ghanaian language is an added advantage.
  • Familiarity with Microsoft Office.
  • Willingness to learn Airtable.

What the Westerwelle Startup Haus Offers

The three National Service positions offer candidates the opportunity to work in a growing international entrepreneurship ecosystem.

Successful candidates can expect exposure to:

1. A New Entrepreneurship Hub

National service candidates will have the opportunity to contribute to the development and growth of one of Ghana’s newest entrepreneurship hubs.

This can provide practical experience in building systems, supporting programmes, engaging members, managing operations, and contributing to an emerging innovation ecosystem.

2. International and Purpose-Driven Work

The Westerwelle Foundation operates internationally, creating an environment where candidates can interact with people and organizations connected to entrepreneurship, innovation, digital transformation, and development.

3. Startup and Innovation Ecosystem Exposure

The positions can provide exposure to:

  • Startups
  • Entrepreneurs
  • Investors
  • Corporates
  • Universities
  • Mentors
  • International partners
  • Innovation organizations
  • Entrepreneurship programmes
  • Ecosystem stakeholders

4. Professional Development

The positions provide practical workplace experience across areas such as:

  • Administration
  • Finance
  • Procurement
  • Programme management
  • Community engagement
  • Marketing
  • Communications
  • Content creation
  • Event coordination
  • Entrepreneurship support

5. International Collaboration

Candidates may also gain exposure to the wider Westerwelle Foundation network and opportunities for collaboration involving stakeholders across Africa and Europe.

6. Collaborative Working Environment

The Foundation describes its team culture as being built around:

  • Trust
  • Ownership
  • Creativity
  • Collaboration
  • Impact

APPLY HERE

Who Can Apply?

These opportunities are specifically targeted at eligible national service candidates for the 2026/2027 cycle.

The required academic background depends on the position.

Operations & Admin Assistant

Applicants should have a Bachelor’s degree or HND in:

  • Accounting
  • Finance
  • Business Administration
  • Logistics
  • A related field

Applicants must also be eligible for the 2026/2027 national service cycle.

Programs Assistant

Applicants should hold a degree in:

  • Business
  • Economics
  • Development Studies
  • Social Sciences
  • Communications
  • A related field

Applicants must also be eligible for the 2026/2027 national service cycle.

Community & Marketing Assistant

Applicants should have a Bachelor’s degree or HND in:

  • Communications
  • Marketing
  • Journalism
  • Hospitality
  • Business Administration
  • A related field

Applicants must also be eligible for the 2026/2027 national service cycle.

Country and Regional Eligibility

The advertised positions are based in Accra, Ghana, and the qualification requirement specifically states that applicants must be eligible national service candidates for the 2026/2027 cycle.

The opportunity is therefore principally intended for candidates who meet Ghana’s national service eligibility requirements. The announcement does not state a particular racial or ethnic restriction.

Candidates should verify their national service eligibility before applying.

Application Deadline

There is no fixed closing date stated for these three positions.

The application deadline is listed as rolling, meaning applications are reviewed as they are received.

Because applications are considered on a rolling basis, interested candidates should avoid waiting until a later date to apply.

How to Apply

Applicants should submit their CV through the relevant application page and complete the application questions associated with the position.

The Foundation states that applications will be reviewed on a rolling basis and that only shortlisted candidates will be contacted.

The organization also aims to provide feedback within two weeks of the application deadline.

How to Prepare a Strong Application

Candidates should tailor their CV to the specific position rather than submitting a generic application.

For the Operations & Admin Assistant role, applicants should emphasize relevant experience in:

  • Administration
  • Finance
  • Excel
  • Procurement
  • Documentation
  • Inventory management
  • Logistics
  • Supplier management
  • Record keeping
  • Office operations

For the Programs Assistant position, applicants should highlight:

  • Programme coordination
  • Event support
  • Research
  • Data management
  • Reporting
  • Excel or Google Sheets
  • Communication
  • Stakeholder engagement
  • Entrepreneurship or development-related experience

For the Community & Marketing Assistant position, applicants should emphasize:

  • Social media management
  • Content creation
  • Photography
  • Videography
  • Video editing
  • Graphic design
  • Canva
  • CapCut
  • Adobe tools, where applicable
  • Website management
  • Digital marketing
  • Community engagement
  • Event coverage
  • Copywriting

Candidates should also ensure that their CV clearly demonstrates their eligibility for the 2026/2027 national service cycle.

Visit HERE to learn more about the Westerwelle Startup Haus Accra National Service Positions 2026/2027.

Conclusion

The Westerwelle Startup Haus Accra is offering three National Service opportunities for the 2026/2027 cycle, covering operations and administration, programme delivery, and community and marketing support.

The three roles provide different pathways into an international entrepreneurship environment. The Operations & Admin Assistant position focuses on facilities, administration, procurement, documentation, and finance support. The Programs Assistant supports programme delivery, participant coordination, reporting, and engagement with founders and facilitators. The Community & Marketing Assistant combines front-of-house responsibilities with social media, content creation, photography, videography, website updates, community engagement, and event support.

With all three positions based in Accra and applications accepted on a rolling basis, eligible national service candidates interested in entrepreneurship, innovation, administration, programmes, communications, marketing, or community engagement can review the relevant requirements and submit their applications through the appropriate position-specific application page.

item.content:encoded:
The King’s Commonwealth Fellowship Programme (KCFP) Undergraduate Fellowships 2027 offer a major opportunity for talented students from eligible Commonwealth Small Island Developing States (SIDS) to pursue undergraduate degrees in their home country or immediate region.

The programme is designed to strengthen local skills, professional capacity and leadership in countries that face significant development challenges, including the growing effects of climate change. Through financial support, professional development and access to an alumni network, the fellowship seeks to equip young people with the knowledge and skills needed to contribute to the long-term development and resilience of their communities.

The 2027 undergraduate fellowship pathway supports students in selected fields including education, engineering, health, environmental health, public health, mathematics education, nursing, sustainable tourism, travel and tourism management, occupational safety and health, geomatics, town and country planning and related disciplines.
